stories.title: Ernie Johnson says this is his final season as 'Inside the NBA' host
stories.summary: Ernie Johnson will retire as host of "Inside the NBA" after the season, saying that it was his decision to step away and that "it's just time."
stories.detailText: Sports Broadcasting Hall of Famer Ernie Johnson will retire as host of "Inside the NBA" after the season, saying in a social media video Wednesday that it was his decision to step away and that "it's just time." Johnson, 70, said he would continue to work, including coverage of the NCAA men's basketball tournament for CBS and Turner Sports. "Just to be clear, I'm not retiring," Johnson said. "Just cutting back. ... So this is by no means the end. It's just a turning of the page. And I'll forever cherish every chapter we have written with 'Inside the NBA.'" Johnson acknowledged that he has dealt with heart issues in recent years. He said that he was doing well but that the health matters helped him realize the importance of time with family, adding "I just want to slow down a bit." "Ernie Johnson is one of sports media's most respected and beloved figures," ESPN chairman Jimmy Pitaro said in a statement. "For more than three decades, he has been the heart of 'Inside the NBA,' helping create one of the most iconic and entertaining studio shows in sports. We are grateful for Ernie's extraordinary contributions and look forward to celebrating him throughout the season." Johnson has worked for Turner Sports since 1989 and began hosting "Inside the NBA" a year later. The show -- led by its current quartet of Johnson, Charles Barkley, Kenny Smith and Shaquille O'Neal -- has won more than 20 Sports Emmy Awards over the decades. The show transitioned from TNT Sports to ESPN and ABC starting last season. Along with Johnson's announcement, Barkley has previously said this will also be his final season on "Inside the NBA," although the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Famer has changed his mind and returned to the desk in previous years. The third edition of "Inside the NBA" on ESPN will be held Wednesday, when the Indiana Pacers host the Philadelphia 76ers (7 p.m. ET) and the Oklahoma City Thunder play at the Dallas Mavericks . The show is set for 25 regular-season appearances in 2026-27 along with the playoffs through the NBA Finals.

stories.title: Timberwolves say Anthony Edwards will be 'good as new' after knee surgery
stories.summary: The Timberwolves believe Anthony Edwards will be "good as new" following arthroscopic surgery for a lingering injury to his right knee.
stories.detailText: MINNEAPOLIS --The Minnesota Timberwolves believe Anthony Edwards will be "good as new" following arthroscopic surgery for a lingering injury to his right knee , president of basketball operations Tim Connelly said Wednesday. Edwards was scheduled for the cleanup procedure Thursday, after which the Timberwolves will have a clearer timetable for his return later this season, whether that becomes a matter of weeks or months. Connelly didn't specify the diagnosis, but Edwards was bothered by right knee pain last spring and limited to a career-low 61 games last season. He then suffered a hyperextension of his left knee in the first round of the playoffs that caused a deep bone bruise and kept him out for two games. Edwards was seen grabbing his knee with a grimace at one point Sunday during the home opener. Even after being listed as questionable to play Monday, Edwards scored 47 points in an overtime loss at Cleveland . His 133 points through four games is a franchise record. An MRI Tuesday revealed new damage for Edwards that was not detected in previous scans, which were done before training camp and during the playoffs. His condition this summer was not such that a procedure would have been recommended then, Connelly said. "He wants to play tonight. He looked pretty good the other night, having the 47," Connelly said before the Timberwolves hosted Golden State. "We're just concerned about his long-term health. We want to make sure we're putting him in the best position he can be so he can be the best version he's going to be for a long time." Edwards, ever the intense competitor, consented to the surgery "kicking and screaming," Connelly said. "He's bummed, but Anthony is such a naturally positive and upbeat guy," Connelly said. "He's hit all his teammates quickly and said, 'You guys got it,' and we'll roll from there." The Timberwolves are already without guard Donte DiVincenzo , who started all 82 games last season before tearing his right Achilles tendon in the same playoff game against Denver during which Edwards hyperextended his left knee. The acquisition of point guard LaMelo Ball remade the lineup and gave the Timberwolves a fresh spark, moving Edwards back to his natural shooting guard spot. There's plenty of backcourt depth with Ayo Dosunmu and Terrence Shannon Jr . coming off the bench so far this season, with one of them likely to start in the absence of Edwards. Another backup, Bones Hyland , will likely have an elevated role as well. "We know he brings dynamic scoring, leadership. Tough to fill in his shoes, just from what he does on the floor for us. Nobody can be like Ant, but we've got players who can step in and just take over a game as well," Hyland said. "Just play team basketball."

stories.detailText: Los Angeles Lakers star Luka Doncic will not play against the LA Clippers on Wednesday at Intuit Dome because of back tightness, the team announced. Doncic scored 41 points in the Lakers' 136-129 home loss to the Portland Trail Blazers on Tuesday -- the team's first loss of the season after a 3-0 start. He leads the league with 36.0 points per game one week into the NBA season. The Lakers, playing on the second night of a back-to-back, will also be down starter Ziaire Williams due to left foot soreness. On the other side, the Clippers will be without forward Rui Hachimura , who has left quad soreness. Kobe Sanders will make his first start of the season in Hachimura's place. Hachimura scored 16 points against his former team last week in the Lakers' 125-117 win over the Clippers at Crypto.com Arena.

stories.detailText: Los Angeles Lakers star Luka Dončić has been ruled out for Wednesday’s game against the L.A. Clippers. Dončić led the Lakers in scoring in a 136-129 home loss to the Portland Trail Blazers on Tuesday, Oct. 27. The point guard nearly produced a double-double with 41 points, nine assists and five rebounds in 39 minutes played against Portland. It followed his 52-point game against the Utah Jazz on Sunday, Oct. 25. Dončić scored 39 points through the first three quarters of play before tying Kareem Abdul-Jabbar with 10 career 50-point games, which is the 11th most in NBA history. The Lakers guard passed Kevin Durant and Giannis Antetokounmpo, who each have nine. Dončić added his name to the franchise record books, becoming the fastest player to score 3,000 points in a Lakers uniform. The six-time All-NBA selection accomplished the feat in 95 games, beating out George Mikan (106) and Abdul-Jabbar (109). Luka Dončić injury update Dončić has been ruled out with back tightness. He was not listed on Monday's injury report ahead of the game against Portland. Coach JJ Redick is expected to talk to the media before tonight's game against the Clippers and will provide an update. stories.title: Former Laker Malik Beasley agrees to plead guilty in federal court over gambling ring involvement
stories.summary: Former NBA player Malik Beasley has agreed to plead guilty in a federal case tied to an alleged gambling ring. He has been accused of illegally manipulating his performance in NBA games.
stories.detailText: Former NBA player Malik Beasley arrives outside of Brooklyn federal court building in July. (Heather Khalifa / Associated Press) Former NBA player Malik Beasley has agreed to a plea deal months after initially pleading not guilty to federal charges tied to his alleged involvement in a gambling ring. Beasley is expected to enter a guilty plea during a Dec. 9 hearing, a spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of New York confirmed in an email to The Times. The NBA journeyman, who spent half of the 2022-2023 season with the Lakers , and several others were charged this summer with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, bribery in sporting contests, honest services wire fraud conspiracy and conspiracy to commit money laundering. Beasley entered a not guilty plea to all charges on July 1. Read more: Former Lakers Malik Beasley and Ed Davis accused of illegal gambling, wire fraud and money laundering It is not clear the charges to which Beasley will be entering a guilty plea. Beasley has been accused of illegally manipulating his performance in NBA games to ensure gamblers won prop bets on at least four occasions while he was playing for the Milwaukee Bucks in 2023-2024. According to the indictment, he and co-defendant Ed Davis , also a one-time Laker who was teammates with Beasley on the 2020-2021 Minnesota Timberwolves, conspired for Beasley to under- or overperform during certain games relative to specific statistics on which others involved in the scheme would place bets. Read more: Marcellus Wiley faces another sexual assault allegation in lawsuit filed by a former USC student Beasley had previously borrowed money from Davis after accumulating millions of dollars in gambling losses. In exchange for fixing his performances, the indictment says, Beasley’s debts to Davis were “reduced or paid off.” Also indicted were Paolo Zamorano, William Brown, Robert Gorodetsky and Ernesto Plascencia. All six defendants initially pleaded not guilty to all charges, but Brown has since pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, and Gorodetsky and Plascencia also both scheduled for change of plea hearings in November. The Associated Press contributed to this report. Get the best, most interesting and strangest stories of the day from the L.A. sports scene and beyond from our newsletter The Sports Report. stories.title: How long could Tyrese Haliburton be out after latest injury setback?
stories.summary: Rick Carlisle and the Pacers are hoping for the best as Tyrese Haliburton deals with a new injury concern. Here's the latest on his status.
stories.detailText: The Indiana Pacers could be without star Tyrese Haliburton again and the NBA might have lost another star player to an injury. The 26-year-old Haliburton is listed as questionable with "left hamstring tightness/soreness" on the team's latest injury report and Pacers coach Rick Carlisle said that Haliburton will meet with an outside specialist before Indiana hosts the Philadelphia 76ers on Oct. 28 . Haliburton had only just made an emotional return after missing the entire 2025-26 season while recovering from a torn Achilles suffered in Game 7 of the 2025 NBA Finals . He played in the Pacers' first four games of the regular season this month, including a back-to-back on Oct. 25-26, and nearly averaged a double-double (21.8 points, 9.5 assists). Here's the latest on Haliburton's injury situation and how it could affect the Pacers season: NBA POWER RANKINGS: Injuries shake up league, winless Miami Heat plummet How long is Tyrese Haliburton out? Haliburton's status moving forward, beginning with Wednesday's game against the 76ers, is "uncertain," according to Carlisle, due to a hamstring injury that surfaced during the first week of the NBA regular season. Carlisle told 107.5 The Fan in Indianapolis that the Pacers guard is consulting with "a hamstring expert" used by the team and will learn more about a potential timetable for his return during a 4:15 p.m. ET meeting that will also involve team management and trainers. "We'll hope this hamstring thing is not a big deal or not any kind of a long term thing," Carlisle said during the interview. Haliburton was seen riding an exercise bike during break in the action in Monday's loss to the Milwaukee Bucks , according to the Indianapolis Star , and said afterwards he felt "banged up." Tyrese Haliburton injury history Haliburton is making a high-profile comeback from his dramatic injury suffered during Game 7 of the 2025 NBA Finals. He did not play during the 2025-26 season while recovering from the Achilles injury. During that process, his progress was slowed by a frustrating case of shingles. Haliburton has also missed time with hamstring issues in the past, including in both the 2023-24 and 2024-25 seasons. But he was in the midst of a successful return through four games this month, emerging again as the Pacers' second-leading scorer and top playmaker. Carlisle had been impressed by the improvements his star had seemingly made in his first appearances since the major injury. "He's got a lot of bounce. He's energetic. He's definitely in an attacking mode and defensively, he's made gains," Carlisle said. "He's gotten stronger and he's battling at a higher level against guys ... A lot of good signs." How Tyrese Haliburton's latest injury impacts Pacers Haliburton's hamstring issues come at an inopportune time for the Pacers. Indiana will already be without center Ivica Zubac (left ankle sprain), backup point guard T.J. McConnell (hamstring strain), guard Ben Sheppard (torn left meniscus) and forward Johnny Furphy (ACL tear) against the Sixers on Wednesday. Guard Andrew Nembhard is listed as questionable with neck stiffness and soreness after missing Monday's game. This would be easier to manage if Indiana were closer to whole. If Haliburton's absence is a few games or a few weeks, the Pacers should still be able to stay afloat and within striking distance of the Eastern Conference playoff picture. But if this turns into another extended absence, Indiana's aspirations to be a contender again become more complicated. The Pacers can survive a short-term setback, but a team built around Haliburton got them to the NBA Finals before and gives them the best chance to do so again in a deeper Eastern Conference. The Timberwolves have a relatively shallow roster, and their bench will be stretched thin once sixth man Ayo Dosunmu moves into the starting lineup to replace Edwards. Their two-way star's absence also reduces any margin for error with the rest of the roster; Ball is notoriously injury-prone, and if both guards are ever out at the same time, a lengthy losing streak could ensue. The rookie extension deadline is not the only date teams are paying attention to, however. He's rolling his sleeves up and getting his hands dirty. He's going to help all of us and probably me, specifically, a ton this year." Donovan joined the staff in July, replacing former lead assistant Sean Sweeney, who left San Antonio to take the head coaching job in Orlando. Sweeney ran the Spurs' defense last season, helping it improve from 25th to third in the NBA in defensive rating (110.4). Donovan won't be tasked with taking on Sweeney's responsibilities, according to sources, however. San Antonio brought in Donovan to lean on his experience on both ends of the floor, as well as his vast knowledge of the NBA and college games. A member of the Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame class of 2025, Donovan joined the Spurs after 11 seasons as an NBA coach with the Chicago Bulls and Oklahoma City Thunder , after capturing two college basketball national titles in 2006 and 2007 with the Florida Gators. -- Michael C. Wright Shead agrees to three-year extension in Toronto Guard Jamal Shead has agreed to a three-year, $24 million extension with the Toronto Raptors , sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. Shead averaged 6.6 points and 5.6 assists per game last season. Sept. 30 Nuggets add Nembhard on two-way deal Guard Ryan Nembhard has agreed to a two-way contract with the Denver Nuggets , sources told ESPN's Shams Charania . Nembhard, 23, played 60 games (27 starts) for the Dallas Mavericks in 2025-26 after signing as an undrafted free agent. He was traded to the Atlanta Hawks then to the Charlotte Hornets this offseason before being waived. Sept. 29 Charania: NBA reviewing finalists' bids for Vegas team ESPN's Shams Charania reported that the NBA is currently reviewing finalist bids for a new expansion team in Las Vegas. The price range is currently speculated at $12-13 billion with a new arena factored into the cost. The three final groups are Nancy Walton Laurie and Bill Laurie; Steve Apostolopoulos and Marc Lasry; Bill Foley and Jerry Colangelo, sources told ESPN. Will KAT take a pay cut in next Knicks deal? On "NBA Today," ESPN's Malika Andrews detailed Karl-Anthony Towns ' mindset toward contract negotiations with the defending champion New York Knicks . "Towns, from what I have been told, is willing -- similarly to what Jalen Brunson did [but the] numbers aren't the same -- to take a pay cut," Andrews said. "But the pay cut that the Knicks are asking him to take, he views as unreasonable." Towns, 30, is eligible to sign a four-year, $276 million extension through June 30. Embiid "full participant" in first Sixers' practice Joel Embiid was a "full participant all the way through" for the Philadelphia 76ers first practice of training camp, Sixers coach Nick Nurse said Tuesday. "He looked great," Nurse said of Embiid. "Very, very good news from the standpoint of where it's been the last couple years, last couple summers leading into today. ... It's great to see." After being named the league MVP in 2023, the 32-year-old center has missed 150 games over the last three seasons because of various injuries. He also sat out four of the Sixers' 11 playoff games in the spring because of appendicitis, right hip soreness and a right ankle sprain. The only Sixers player who did not participate in Tuesday's practice according to a team spokesperson was backup big man Adem Bona , who is dealing with a sprained left foot. Anfernee Simons , who signed a two-year, $12.3 million contract to join Philadelphia in July, said Embiid's presence in the gym was already notable leading up to the start of camp. "Everybody's been impressed around here about how he's come in and worked," Simons said. "Joel is going to be Joel. He's going to be a dominant player always. We just want to continue for him to be himself, as well, and I think everybody's going to be able to work around that." Despite the injuries, the 10-year veteran still averaged 26.9 points, 7.7 rebounds, 3.9 assists and 1.2 blocks per game last season. Embiid's inclusion only added to what several Sixers players described as an "exciting" opening day with LeBron James and Jaylen Brown completing their first official practice with the franchise. "With any team, we got to start somewhere, and then we got to get better and better, and just keep trying to reach our ceiling, right?" Nurse said. "That happens day-to-day. Can we get up tomorrow, like, 98% as excited as we did today? It's going to be hard to get as excited as we all were today, right? "But we need to come back, and we need to keep climbing that mountain. That's a daily process. I just want them to reach their potential. If they do, great things are going to happen." -- Dave McMenamin Hoop Collective: The 2026 NBA Media Day reaction special Brian Windhorst is joined by ESPN reporters from around the league to check in on Monday's Media Days. Tim MacMahon, Dave McMenamin, Vince Goodwill, Jamal Collier, Anthony Slater and Michael C. Wright all hop on the podcast to discuss the biggest storylines throughout the NBA ahead of training camp. "He said, 'I would like to stay in New York for the rest of my career.' And then he kind of ended it and because of the way the Knicks operated, it wasn't like you had space for a follow-up. "And then someone else, I think Ian Begley asked him, 'Are you OK with playing this out through the season or do you want to table contract talks?' and he basically said, 'Everybody's going to be a little uncomfortable around here.'" Latest episodes of the 'Hoop Collective' podcast Top NBA media day headlines LeBron says he envisioned joining Knicks as free agent | Philly stars ready to 'sacrifice' Clippers apologize to fans, vow to move past investigation | Ingram (Achilles) out Edwards happy to cede Wolves' PG duties to Ball Wizards, AD to wait until summer for extension talks Karl-Anthony Towns wants extension to stay with Knicks Jokic on his next Nuggets deal: 'I'm going to sign next year' Bronny on LeBron James' Lakers exit: 'He's got his own path' Sept. 28 Bronny on LeBron James' Lakers exit: 'He's got his own path' When LeBron James chose to leave the Los Angeles Lakers in free agency over the summer, he consulted his family on the decision to sign with the Philadelphia 76ers . But when it came to his son/teammate Bronny, much was apparently left unsaid . "We're men of very little words when it comes to talking about business and what we're going to do and how we feel about each other. So it wasn't really much [discussion] to be honest with you," Bronny James said Monday at Lakers media day. "He's got his own path and I got my own. He knows that I want to make a name for myself and I want to continue my career and keep growing as a player. And he knows that I want to focus on that. So he decided to do that." LeBron and Bronny have routinely been in unique situations in league history, whether it was opening night two years ago, when the father and son entered the game together, or last year in the playoffs, where they combined to deliver a 10-0 run during a victory over the Houston Rockets . Navigating a complex free agency in which the father leaves and the son stays is another one for the books. Tatum 'comfortable' leading new-look Celtics post-Brown trade Jayson Tatum 's one constant during his development into a star with the Boston Celtics was having Jaylen Brown as a teammate. That partnership ended this offseason when the Celtics' front office decided to trade Brown -- the 2024 NBA Finals MVP -- to the Philadelphia 76ers in what was largely a cost-cutting move that broke up the duo most responsible for leading Boston to the 2024 NBA championship. "The business of the NBA comes and plays a part at some point. And I've seen it in my almost 10 years in this league," Tatum said during Celtics media day on Monday . "For me it's more so being grateful for what we accomplished and what he means for this city and to this organization. Just the ups and downs in our career that we were able to grow and learn from and made us the players that we are today. So really just being thankful for those nine years." Suns owner Ishbia says mortgage company woes won't hurt team It's well-known at this point that billionaire Mat Ishbia's mortgage company has had a rough financial stretch. The owner of the Phoenix Suns said Monday that will have "zero" effect on his spending habits when it comes to basketball. In fact, the 46-year-old said he's working on purchasing 14% more of the team, bringing his total to roughly 80%. Ishbia's company -- United Wholesale Mortgage -- suffered a reported $450 million net loss in the second quarter this year, calling into question if the sizable dip would affect his basketball business. The outspoken Ishbia was adamant that nothing would change for the NBA franchise when it comes to spending on players or the fan experience. Williamson not where he wants to be New Orleans Pelicans forward Zion Williamson kept his answer brief when asked how he would summarize his first seven years as an NBA player. "I'm not where I want to be," said Williamson, whom the Pelicans drafted with the No. 1 pick out of Duke in 2019. "I'm not where I need to be." Butler indicates he is 'ahead' in his knee rehab Nearing the eight-month mark since his right ACL surgery , Jimmy Butler III is hesitant to put a specific target date on his eventual NBA return, but he did express optimism in advance of Golden State Warriors training camp. "I promise you I'm coming back, and it's going to be -- I think it's going to be, like, real eye-popping for everybody how I'm still going to be nice," Butler said. "Probably nicer, honestly." Butler has only recently advanced to running, and he will be limited to light on-court individual work when the team begins practice in Hawaii on Tuesday afternoon. It will be several weeks before Butler is expected to advance to a more rigorous stage of his rehab, and the team's lead medical decision-maker, Rick Celebrini, is known for his cautiousness in the later stages of the rehab process. A January or February return can be considered on the optimistic side for Butler, who turned 37 earlier this month. But Butler did say that the strengthening tests on the knee indicate he is ahead of schedule. "My numbers are staggering," Butler said. "They're off the charts. I'm ahead, so they say. So, I just know that all the work that I've been doing, whether it be at home, in L.A., in Europe, in South America, wherever the case may be, I've been doing all the right things. So, I am confident that whenever I come back, I'll be more than ready, I'll be more than healthy and I'll be a better all-around player than I was whenever I went down." -- Anthony Slater Pistons eye "better version" of Cunningham Detroit Pistons coach J.B. Bickerstaff has held many offseason conversations with All-NBA guard Cade Cunningham about seizing greatness and the necessary steps toward improving after last year's playoff run that stretched to Game 7 of the Eastern Conference semifinals. Bickerstaff has guaranteed "a better version" Cunningham this season, which could be a scary sight after he averaged 23.9 points, 9.9 assists, 5.5 rebounds and 1.4 steals in 33.9 minutes during 2025-26. But Cunningham also led the East in turnovers per game after finishing with the second most in 2024-25. "I don't have to challenge Cade, and that's why he is who he is," Bickerstaff said. "Because he's pulling. He's not being pushed." Cunningham showed up in a fresh pair of Nike S.T. Charge "Detroit Tough" sneakers in Pistons colors. He will also receive his own signature Nike shoe, which is expected to debut during the second half of the season. "I'm thankful to be in these shoes. I'm thankful to have the opportunity to represent my family in this way," Cunningham said. "Represent where I come from, but then to represent the city of Detroit. "In a city like this, it's a blessing. I'm thankful for it, I don't take it for granted and I'm trying to make the most out of it." -- Eric Woodyard Hornets waive former No. 8 pick Dillingham The Charlotte Hornets are waiving guard Rob Dillingham , sources told ESPN's Shams Charania . Dillingham was traded from the Chicago Bulls on Saturday for Buddy Hield and cash. The Hornets created a $9.6 million trade exception with the move. Dillingham, 21, appeared in 30 games for the Bulls last season, averaging 9.6 points and 2.8 assists. SGA on chance at historic third straight MVP At Oklahoma City Thunder media day, guard Shai Gilgeous-Alexander discussed the possibility of winning a third straight NBA MVP award and whether that's something he ponders going into this season. "No different than any other year: Try to be the best player I can be, try to implement the things I just worked on," Gilgeous-Alexander said. "The decision for MVP is literally 82 games away. I'm not going to win the award in the first week of the season. ... That kind of recipe for me in the past has kind of worked, and I've been fortunate to win two in a row. "We need to be laser focused on ourselves. We need to take the lessons from that [Western Conference finals] series, for sure, and we did. But it's certainly not something that we overcorrect for, because you end up chasing your shadow, and it prevents you from being your best as you move forward." ESPN's Summer Forecast gave Gilgeous-Alexander the fourth-best chance at the 2027 MVP, behind Victor Wembanyama , Nikola Jokic and Luka Doncic . No player has won three consecutive MVPs since Larry Bird in 1984, 1985 and 1986. -- Baxter Holmes Doncic talks LeBron exit, Lakers "championship" ceiling Speaking to ESPN's Brian Windhorst during Los Angeles Lakers media day, guard Luka Doncic detailed his reaction to LeBron James leaving for the Philadelphia 76ers this past summer and why he thinks a successful 2026-27 includes a Lakers run to the title: "It was kind of sad. Playing with LeBron was amazing. There's a lot of things I learned from him. ... We all know who LeBron James is." Shams: Duren's relationship with Pistons "has fractures" Simmons "didn't touch a ball for a year" During Sacramento Kings media day, guard Ben Simmons laid out the reasons he chose the Kings and why he's excited for the 2026-27 season. "The expectations are low. I feel like that's been something on me too, so we can relate in that way," Simmons told reporters. "I think we have a chip on our shoulder." Simmons last played in 2024-25, appearing in 51 games for the Brooklyn Nets and LA Clippers . The three-time All-Star said the time away gave him the chance to focus on "getting my body right and my mind right." Pistons GM hasn't spoken with Duren all summer Jalen Duren and the Detroit Pistons have a decision to make as the clock ticks closer to Oct. 1 -- the deadline to sign a one-year, $9.6 million qualifying offer. For Duren, he can accept the five-year, $200 million contract that has been offered by Detroit or he can become the first player named All-NBA or All-Star to sign the qualifying offer. If he chooses the latter, Duren will hold veto power on any trade this season and be an unrestricted free agent next summer. For the Pistons, weighing the risk of having an All-NBA player on a one-year contract and, more importantly, the likelihood he will depart next summer as a free agent is key. There are eight projected teams that have significant cap space to sign Duren to a four-year, $189 million max contract. "I can't control the different things that he does or his group does," Pistons president of basketball operations Trajan Langdon said at media day. "For me, it's control what we can and letting him know he is a big part of what we do." Langdon also said he hasn't spoken with Duren all summer during Pistons media day. -- Bobby Marks Mitchell: LeBron to Cavs made sense "for a lot of reasons" At Cavaliers media day, Donovan Mitchell said that in his mind, he thought LeBron James would return to Cleveland because "for a lot of reasons it made sense." "I didn't think Philly. I thought if he didn't come here, it'd be Golden State," Mitchell said. After being swept in the Eastern Conference finals by the eventual champion New York Knicks then missing out on James in free agency, Cleveland kept its core intact. The Cavs signed Mitchell to a four-year, $273 million maximum extension and re-signed James Harden to a three-year, $97 million contract. Cleveland did make one major addition by acquiring Peyton Watson from the Denver Nuggets in a multiteam trade then signing the restricted free agent to a four-year, $88 million deal. Speaking for the first time since their extensions, Mitchell and Harden both said their approaches to their new deals -- Mitchell signing as soon as he was eligible with Harden opting out to give Cleveland more flexibility to make moves -- reflected a team-first mindset. "This is something that I want to do, and I want to win a championship," Harden said. "So, what does that look like? Making the team better, making the team whole to where we give ourselves a chance. By the way, you can have the best talented team, which I've been on before, and still not win. "We waited, waited, waited until the front office called me, made sure that we got everything that we can get, and then we signed. We got a long way to go, but I love the direction and steps that we're taking here as a unit from top to bottom." -- Daniel Oyefusi MacMahon: Thunder adjusting to roster changes The departures of three championship-winning teammates doesn't yet feel like reality for Thunder superstar Shai Gilgeous-Alexander , who kidded that he still expected Luguentz Dort , Isaiah Joe and Aaron Wiggins to show up for Oklahoma City's team picture Monday afternoon. "It's the business of the NBA, right?" Gilgeous-Alexander said, referring to the series of financially motivated trades. "I don't think anybody has played with all 12 guys their whole career. It sucks a little bit. "My mind never even went to what we were going to be like on the court. It was more like the brotherhood." As fellow OKC guard Jalen Williams added, "It's the weirdest thing ever." -- Tim MacMahon Clippers announce Ingram has partially torn Achilles The LA Clippers announced they found a partially torn Achilles tendon in Brandon Ingram 's foot after his recent heel surgery. He will miss the start of the 2026-27 season. Jokic: "I'm gonna sign next year" Denver Nuggets center Nikola Jokic reiterated his commitment to the franchise at Monday's media day. "I'm gonna sign next year," Jokic said. "If they want me." Curry said knee is ready to go for the season Golden State Warriors superstar guard Stephen Curry addressed the media Monday in offering positive updates on his injured knee. "Knee's feeling great. Ready to go. No issues," Curry said. "I feel a lot stronger and understanding of what I'm dealing with." Curry did acknowledge a "management element" but said there are currently no restrictions. Nuggets confident in Jokic's future with franchise Members of the Denver Nuggets ' front office, general manager Jon Wallace and executive vice president of basketball Ben Tenzer addressed the media on Monday and answered questions regarding Nikola Jokic 's future with the franchise. The three-time MVP didn't sign an extension this offseason. "We feel very comfortable with the relation and trust there," Tenzer said. "We have no concerns." LeBron: I wanted to finish my career with the Knicks New Philadelphia 76er LeBron James said his decision came down to five teams this offseason and that he envisioned going to the New York Knicks before they won the 2026 title. "I had visions of playing in [Madison Square] Garden and finishing my career in the Garden," James told ESPN on Monday during the 76ers' media day. "One of the best places I've ever played. "I think it's the No. 1 arena in the world, as far as for a basketball player. But after they beat San Antonio, I was like, 'Hey, I can't.' I couldn't do it." James and the 76ers will play the Knicks at the Garden on opening night, Oct. 20. No update on Gary Trent Jr. investigation Milwaukee Bucks governor Wes Edens did not provide an update on the league investigation into Gary Trent Jr. 's contract. "I don't have any update," Edens said. "We're working with the league and fully cooperating with them. But I don't have any insight beyond that." The NBA is looking into a potential cap-circumvention violation by the Bucks around Trent's deal this offseason. Cronin: Blazers have "belief" in Ja Morant Portland Trail Blazers ' general manager Joe Cronin addressed why the franchise decided to trade for Ja Morant this offseason during Portland's media day on Monday. "Just straight belief in Ja," Cronin said. "Our view of Ja as still a very high-level player. "I'm sure there will be questions about fit, but we're very focused on talent." Cronin also said veteran guard Jrue Holiday could play some minutes on the wing for Portland this season, while adding that Holiday and veteran guard Damian Lillard will have a positive influence on Morant. Kerr: Rookie Lendeborg going to "play a ton" Golden State Warriors coach Steve Kerr said during Monday's media day that he expects rookie Yaxel Lendeborg to "play a ton" this season. "He's clearly going to play a ton," Kerr said. "He gives us the size and the versatility that we need. "Whether he's a starter or coming off the bench, that will be determined the next couple of weeks." Lendeborg was the No. 11 pick in the 2026 NBA draft and averaged 15.1 points per game at Michigan last season. Embiid: 'Extremely excited' about this year's team Philadelphia 76ers center Joel Embiid said Monday that he feels like the team finally has the right mix of players, after an offseason in which the franchise traded for Jaylen Brown and signed LeBron James to join the young guard tandem of VJ Edgecombe and Tyrese Maxey . "It's hard to win when you get a group of guys together for one year, two years, maybe," he said. "I'm extremely excited about this team because we have the right mix of veteran leadership and younger guys. We might have some ups and downs, but we're gonna get there." Wembanyama addresses last year's Finals loss After leading by double digits in each of the five games in last season's NBA Finals, San Antonio Spurs center Victor Wembanyama said his memories of it will fuel the team this season. "I couldn't imagine a better motivation," he said. Harper addresses role for coming season After offseason chatter about his role, San Antonio Spurs guard Dylan Harper said he'd follow the coaches' lead this season. "Everyone has a competitive edge to them. But the biggest thing for me is whatever I can do, just like last year, to help the team win," he said. "Whatever position the coaches think is best for me to be in, that's the position I'll happily go in." First look at LeBron in a 76ers uniform New Philadelphia 76ers forward LeBron James is taking questions from reporters on Monday. Here's what he had to say when asked about his initial impressions of his team: "Everybody is on the same page," James said. "We are all speaking the same language." LeBron addressed his role too, saying he's open to whatever the team needs from him to win. "Whatever they need me to do," he said. "The luxury of my game is I can do everything. ... Literally, I can do everything" Kawhi: I was a distraction, ready to move forward In his first public appearance with the Toronto Raptors after a controversy-filled summer, Kawhi Leonard addressed the NBA's investigation into him and his business dealings. "I know why some of you guys came. You want to hear about the investigation. But in talking with the NBA and PA, I think the best decision is to move forward and focus on my time being a Toronto Raptor," he said. "I already was a distraction for the past 70 days and wasn't able to meet my teammates or do any of that stuff, minicamp stuff, so, moving forward, I just want to talk about the Toronto Raptors." Haliburton: I am 100% healthy Indiana Pacers guard Tyrese Haliburton said Monday that he is healthy and ready for the season. "I am healthy. I am 100%," he said. "There will be no restrictions. That is not news. There is no source. I am the source. I am ready to go for the year." Porzingis out indefinitely in blow to Warriors Golden State Warriors big man Kristaps Porzingis is out indefinitely to open training camp with a health issue, according to the team. In late July, Porzingis agreed to a two-year, $40 million contract with a player option on the second season to return to the Warriors. Brown: KAT, Hart extension talks won't be a distraction After reports surfaced last week that negotiations between the New York Knicks and center Karl-Anthony Towns had hit a stalemate, coach Mike Brown said Monday neither Towns' situation nor Hart's would linger in the locker room. "We talk about everything [with the team]," Brown said. "We don't want to have any elephants in the room." "I'm not involved in it. They'll figure it out. Control what you can control." And here's what Towns said about a potential extension: "I've made it known I want to play here. Been a fan since I was a kid. I'd like to get it done." Hornets GM: Brandon Miller to be ready for training camp After undergoing offseason surgery on his left shoulder, Hornets wing Brandon Miller should be a full participant in training camp and "ready to roll" for opening night, Hornets general manager Jeff Peterson said Monday. Miller, 23, is entering his fourth NBA season after being the No. 2 pick in the 2023 draft. Duren won't be at Pistons media day, start of camp Detroit Pistons All-Star center Jalen Duren is not attending the team's media day on Monday or the start of training camp as his contract standoff continues, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania on Monday. Duren, a restricted free agent, is declining the team's five-year, $200 million fully guaranteed offer as both sides remain at a stalemate ahead of the Thursday deadline on a one-year, $9.6 million qualifying offer, sources said. Sept. 26 Bulls trade Dillingham to Hornets for Hield, cash The Chicago Bulls and Charlotte Hornets agreed to a trade sending Rob Dillingham to Charlotte for Buddy Hield and cash, the teams announced Saturday. 2026 NBA offseason trade grades Sept. 25 What's next for Curry and the Warriors? Stephen Curry 's two-year, $116 million extension made him the first player in NBA history to amass $600 million in career on-court earnings. The deal has also put the Golden State Warriors in position to have extra spending power next summer. By Curry taking $10 million less than the maximum allowed, the Warriors project to have nearly $38 million in cap space in 2027. Golden State could increase its projection to $55 million if center Kristaps Porzingis is waived in the offseason. Porzingis' $20 million salary for next season is guaranteed for $3 million. For Golden State to have ample room, forwards Draymond Green and Jimmy Butler III would need to sign elsewhere or at a significantly lesser salary. They will be free agents next summer. Both salary projections include the $17 million free agent hold of guard Brandin Podziemski . The 2023 first-round pick is eligible until Oct. 19 to extend his contract. -- Bobby Marks Grading the Curry deal: Why Warriors don't get an A Hornets star Knueppel sidelined by hamstring injury The Charlotte Hornets announced that Kon Knueppel will be out for at least the entire preseason because of a left hamstring injury. James: Maxey, Embiid were factors in joining 76ers LeBron James said his longstanding friendship with All-Star Tyrese Maxey and a desire to help Joel Embiid win his first NBA title played significant roles in his decision to sign a two-year, $8 million contract with the Philadelphia 76ers in July. "[Embiid has] done everything in our league, and the only thing he has not done is win a championship. And I want to try to help him get that first one," James said. "He has a city on his back. He's been 'The Process' for 10 years, 12 years, however long he's been there. But I think it's time we even get you deeper into the process. And I hope that I can be, kind of, that final little piece that can help him get over the hump." Grizzlies waive Russell The Memphis Grizzlies have waived D'Angelo Russell , sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. Russell has made one All-Star team during his career and was selected No. 2 in the 2015 NBA draft.

stories.title: Wizards upgrade No. 1 pick AJ Dybantsa to available vs. Cavaliers
stories.summary: Wizards rookie AJ Dybantsa, who has missed the first four games of the season with an ankle injury, has been upgraded to available for Wednesday's matchup against the Cavaliers.
stories.detailText: Washington Wizards rookie AJ Dybantsa is set to make his NBA regular-season debut Wednesday night against the Cleveland Cavaliers . Dybantsa, the first overall pick in June's NBA draft, has been upgraded to available after missing the first four games of the Wizards' season as he recovered from an ankle injury he suffered in Washington's preseason finale on Oct. 16. The team put out a short social media post -- "no more waiting" -- on Wednesday in anticipation of Dybantsa's return. The 19-year old chimed in a short time later, stating simply, "it's time." The Wizards are off to a 2-2 start to the season without the services of their highly touted rookie. The Wizards also announced Wednesday that forward Justin Champagnie had a surgical procedure to repair a fracture in his right foot, an injury he sustained in Monday's game against the Charlotte Hornets . A timetable for his return was not immediately disclosed. Dybantsa averaged 13 points, 4.3 rebounds, 2.3 assists and two steals in three preseason appearances, while shooting just over 42% from the floor. The 6-foot-9 forward out of BYU averaged 25.5 points, 6.8 rebounds, 3.7 assists and 1.1 steals per game while shooting 51% from the field in his lone college season in Provo.

stories.title: Can these Timberwolves keep pace in the West without Anthony Edwards?
stories.summary: Minnesota's massive summertime pivot was working before its superstar went down with a knee injury.
stories.detailText: It was working. The whole idea behind the Minnesota Timberwolves' massive summertime pivot — out go Julius Randle and Naz Reid, in comes LaMelo Ball — was to find a way to reduce the ball-handling and shot-creation workload on Anthony Edwards, and allow the four-time All-Star to do what he does best: put the ball in the basket, again and again and again. And through four games of the 2026-27 NBA season, it was working . Edwards opened the season on fire, scoring more points per game than anybody besides Luka Dončić, while shooting 54% on 2-pointers and 40% from long distance. He's been at his most efficient with Ball setting him up, posting an absurd 75% true shooting percentage (which factors in 2-point, 3-point and free-throw accuracy) with Ball on the floor , 20 percentage points above his career average; LaMelo-to-Ant has produced more baskets (10) than any other assist combination in the league thus far. The Wolves enter Wednesday's matchup with the Golden State Warriors owning the NBA's No. 4 offense and leading the league in both pull-up field-goal attempts and pull-up shooting efficiency , with Edwards and Ball leading the way. Minnesota is scoring a scorching 126.8 points per 100 non-garbage-time possessions with its new-look backcourt on the floor, opening the season with three blowout wins and an overtime loss against a Cleveland Cavaliers squad that just made the Eastern Conference finals. The vibes between LaMelo Ball and Anthony Edwards were strong early on. (Photo by Erick W. Rasco/Sports Illustrated via Getty Images) Erick W. Rasco via Getty Images This, broadly, is the formula that the Wolves believed would give them the brand of firepower necessary to be able to more effectively stand toe-to-toe with the likes of the Oklahoma City Thunder and San Antonio Spurs, who have eliminated them from the last two postseasons. It's a formula, however, that requires Edwards to remain upright and ambulatory … and, as we learned on Tuesday, that's something he's not going to be for a while . Just four games into the season, Edwards needs arthroscopic surgery on his right knee — the same knee in which he experienced recurring issues last season with what's called patellofemoral pain syndrome, or "runner's knee." That ailment cost the All-NBA guard 11 of the Wolves' final 14 games of the regular season; he needed to have his right knee drained multiple times during Minnesota's playoff run , too. (He also hyperextended his left knee during the opening round against the Denver Nuggets; he missed just two games, and averaged 23.7 points on 47/38/80 shooting splits after returning.) After spending the bulk of the summer resting up to give that knee time to properly heal , and reportedly feeling fully healthy and operational through Minnesota's training camp and preseason slate, Edwards reportedly tweaked his knee during the Wolves' opening-night win over the Miami Heat. You'd be forgiven for not noticing, considering he hung 45 and drilled nine 3-pointers to ruin Giannis Antetokounmpo's South Beach debut: Despite the tweak, Edwards played on, with observers noticing frequent grimacing , instinctive reaches for that right knee , and the occasional limp. But while he was listed as questionable heading into Monday's matchup with the Cavaliers, Edwards not only played, but logged 41 minutes, had more total touches ( 82 ) and a higher time of possession ( nine minutes ) than any other player in the game, and finished nearly 40% of Minnesota's offensive possessions with a shot attempt, foul drawn or turnover — a usage rate that would've been a top-five mark for him in each of the last four seasons — all on the second night of a back-to-back. In fairness, he did look awfully good while doing so … … and the Wolves, it seems, didn't suspect that there was anything more significant going on than the kind of soreness through which superstars of Edwards' caliber are often expected to play. "It's a daily situation," Wolves head coach Chris Finch told reporters before the Cavs game. "I don't think there's any long-term concern." Concerns mounted after the game, though, with subsequent imaging showing "increased issues there," according to ESPN's Shams Charania — damage "that was different from what he experienced against the San Antonio Spurs in May," according to Jon Krawczynski of The Athletic. "It's not a meniscus," Wolves president of basketball operations Tim Connelly told reporters at the team's Wednesday shootaround session. "It's just a — I don't want to speak out of school. My liberal arts degree will screw me up. It's just an arthroscopic clean-up of his knee. … We've had a bunch of imaging since the summer, and it changed as of yesterday." Based on that new information, player and team elected to move forward with a surgical procedure on Thursday, from which Sarah Todd of the Minnesota Star Tribune reports that the Wolves "hope to have [Edwards] back on the court sometime in December." That might be a tad optimistic. Krawczynski pegs Edwards' return as more likely to be in January : "As of now, the belief is it's going to be more than two months ." Two months from Thursday would be Dec. 29. The Wolves' final game of 2026 comes on New Year's Eve at home against the Denver Nuggets. If Edwards is back for that, he would have missed 28 games, ensuring that, for the second consecutive year , he'll be ineligible for year-end awards like Most Valuable Player and the All-NBA teams, and for the supermax salary escalators on his next extension that would come if he were to receive them. The message coming out of Minnatlantasota , though, is that Ant is focused less on putting himself in position to make the top dollar next summer than giving himself the best chance to reach the top of the mountain this spring. "Like we've talked about before, there's only one thing that matters to Ant," Justin Holland, Edwards' business manager, said in a statement to The Athletic . "It's not about individual accolades, All-NBAs or anything like that. It's a single focus: winning a championship. We've seen in a short time what this team is capable of, and know big things are ahead when all are 100%." That could be especially true in a Western Conference in which the Thunder will likely be without starters Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace for most, if not all, of the regular season , and in which a Spurs team that opened up with losses to Oklahoma City and Houston might have some kinks to iron out as they look to return to the NBA Finals. If the expected powerhouses have more cracks in the armor than might have been anticipated, and if Edwards and the Wolves believe that what they put on tape during those first four games is real, then nothing matters more than entering the postseason as close to full strength as possible — even if that means putting Edwards on ice. "With Anthony, all he wants to do is compete, so he's doing this kicking and screaming," Connelly said Wednesday. "But we're pretty confident that he'll get out there when he's right. We don't know when it's going to be, but we don't think it's going to be something that's going to cost him the season. … The best thing about what he's gonna go under is, he'll be as good as new. It's not something we're concerned with long term." Of course, the rest of the Wolves still have to make it through these next two months without falling too far off the pace in the West. You don't just replace a player who can average more than 30 points per game while soaking up nearly 40% of the team's offensive possessions; it'll be interesting to see how Finch rebalances the books to keep Minnesota's attack humming. You'd expect Jaden McDaniels, who saw his per-possession scoring and usage rate both climb last season when he wasn't playing alongside Edwards — and who opened eyebrows with his 32-point, 10-rebound performance to close out Denver in Game 6 of the opening round with Edwards sidelined — to play a larger finishing role, too. You'd expect Ball — who, through four games, is scoring, shooting and using a lower share of his team's offensive possessions than he has since his rookie year in Charlotte — to scale his usage back up toward the No. 1 option levels of his latter years with the Hornets. You'd expect the Wolves to push the pace even more, too. Minnesota has gotten out in transition less frequently in recent years with Edwards on the floor than when he sits , and a more Ball-centric approach would seem to be one oriented more toward hitting the gas than to patiently probing in the half-court. "I think it's more pace now," reserve guard Bones Hyland told reporters on Wednesday. "More running, a lot more up-and-down, and a lot more excitement as well. A lot of players stepping up. We got a lot of versatility, so I think it's gonna be good for us." Ayo Dosunmu, recipient of a nine-figure contract this summer , will likely slide into the starting lineup and shoulder some of the shot-creation workload. Jonathan Kuminga, off to such a strong start doing the dirty work as a complementary two-way power forward, could be asked to step into more shots. Finch will need more from reserves like Hyland, Terrence Shannon Jr., Jaylen Clark and, frankly, everyone else — including Rudy Gobert and Joan Beringer, the back-line anchors of a defense that will have to remain among the NBA's elite for the Wolves to consistently notch Ws in the absence of their most dangerous offensive weapon. Edwards, evidently, is confident in their ability to hold down the fort without a top-10 player in the world. It's kind of ironic: What Edwards saw in these first four games made him believe enough in the potential of who the Wolves could grow to be that he's willing to sacrifice the next couple of months in hopes of maximizing their opportunity of reaching that vaulted ceiling.

stories.title: Ziaire Williams defended himself after receiving flopping technical foul
stories.summary: Williams has dealt with flopping infractions in consecutive games
stories.detailText: SALT LAKE CITY, UT - OCTOBER 25: Ziaire Williams #11 of the Los Angeles Lakers looks on during the game against the Utah Jazz on October 25, 2026 at Delta Center in Salt Lake City, Utah. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this Photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Alex Goodlett/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images Midway through the fourth quarter of the Los Angeles Lakers’ 136-129 loss to the Portland Trail Blazers Tuesday night, three flopping technicals were doled out in a 90-second span. The first culprit was Toumani Camara while he guarded Luka Dončić on an inbounds play. Then, Ja Morant ricocheted off of Austin Reaves as he recovered around a screen. Thirteen seconds later, Ziaire Williams wobbled in retreat after forcing Deni Avdija away from his preferred right hand and received a forearm to the sternum. The refs called THREE flopping technicals in 2 minutes 😭 pic.twitter.com/eAeeSN9Prz — BrickCenter (@BrickCenter_) October 28, 2026 Among the three infractions, Williams certainly has the clearest case for frustration. Avdija absolutely pushes him and is already a much stronger player than Williams. Williams flailing his arms doesn’t do him any favors in the officials’ eyes. But that’s much more about him trying to stay upright and on his feet rather than convincing anyone of an offensive foul and he immediately darts right back into the play to defend Avdija. After the game, Williams took exception to the tech and explained his perspective. “I mean, if the dude was pushing off me, my body is naturally going to waver back,” Williams told reporters. “I don’t know. I didn’t think I flopped. I don’t know, man. I don’t know.” On Monday, Williams received a $2,000 flopping fine for a similar play to Tuesday’s event. Against the Utah Jazz on Sunday, he cut off a Keyonte George drive and took a forearm to the hip, which sent him stumbling backward. That time, George was called for an offensive foul but Williams “was assessed a postgame Flopping fine of $2,000 upon league office review.” LAL’s Ziaire Williams was assessed a postgame Flopping fine of $2,000 upon league office review for https://t.co/gJPymw7mOP on Oct. 25 vs. UTA. Flopping is among the NBA’s Areas of Focus for the 2026-27 season. — NBA Official (@NBAOfficial) October 27, 2026 Williams maintains he is not flopping, and it’s hard to really contend otherwise. He’s a pretty slight-of-frame defender moving backward against players extending their arms into him. He does not want to fall over and miss out on the play, so he uses his arms to keep on his feet. That’s simple physics. “They’ve just been calling it. I haven’t heard anything from anyone,” Williams said. “Like I said, I don’t think I’m flopping. If I was flopping, I’d be on the floor. But it is what it is. Nothing I can do about it now.” Despite the recent, frustrating flopping incidents, Williams is off to an excellent start with the Lakers. Through four games, he’s averaging 11.3 points, 3.0 rebounds, 2.3 assists and 1.5 steals while shooting 69.2% on 2-pointers and 46.7% beyond the arc. He’ll look to continue his rhythm and avoid any harsh flopping calls Wednesday night as the Lakers take on the Clippers at 7:30 p.m. You can follow Jackson on Twitter at @jackfrank_jjf .

stories.title: Pacers' Tyrese Haliburton to miss time with strained hamstring
stories.summary: Haliburton joins a frighteningly long list of NBA stars injured to start the season.
stories.detailText: Pacers star point guard Tyrese Haliburton is joining a frighteningly long list of NBA stars missing time with injuries in the first week of the season. Haliburton has suffered a left hamstring strain and will miss time, a story first reported by ESPN’s Shams Charania . How much time will depend on the severity of the strain. Pacers coach Rick Carlisle added this in an interview on 1075 The Fan , via Tony East : "We'll hope this hamstring thing is not a big deal or not any kind of a long-term thing. But as I said, we'll know more about that later this evening." It's worth noting that teams are cautious about bringing back players from hamstring strains, as they are particularly susceptible to re-injury. Haliburton had returned to the Pacers this season after missing all of last season with a torn Achilles suffered in Game 7 of the 2025 NBA Finals. Through four games this season, Haliburton was averaging 21.8 points and 9.5 assists a night. Indiana has dealt with a rash of injuries at the start of the season — four of their five ideal starters are on the injury report. For Wednesday night's game, Ivica Zubac (ankle), Ben Sheppard (meniscus tear), T.J. McConnell (hamstring), and Johnny Furphy (ACL) are out, and Andrew Nembhard is questionable with neck stiffness. Haliburton joins a too-long list of NBA stars missing time with injuries to start the season: Jalen Williams, Anthony Edwards, Cason Wallace, Kawhi Leonard, Jalen Duren, Paolo Banchero, Jalen Suggs, and Jaren Jackson Jr., just to name a few. That's not counting guys such as Kon Knueppel or Tobias Harris, who have yet to play due to minor injuries. At least No. 1 pick AJ Dybantsa will make his debut Wednesday.

stories.title: Pistons' physical identity makes them a great team, but does it also hurt their title chances?
stories.summary: Eric Samulski dissects the Detroit Pistons' identity and what might need to change for them to win an NBA title
stories.detailText: Before the Detroit Pistons took on the New York Knicks at Madison Square Garden on Tuesday night, Pistons head coach J.B. Bickerstaff talked about the team's dedication to playing "Pistons basketball." Then, seated in the same folding chair only a few hours later, after the Pistons fell to the Knicks 111-97, Bickerstaff wondered if the NBA was unfairly penalizing the Pistons for being who they are. "It is extremely frustrating. To see it happen the way that it happens. There is a discrepancy," Bickerstaff said, about the way his team is officiated. "There's a physicality that we play with and play with every night, and the League should be accustomed to it by now. We've been doing it for three years, and it's not going to change." That physicality is part of what Bickerstaff referred to pre-game as "Pistons basketball." Since being hired by the team in the summer of 2024, Bickerstaff and his staff have created an identity that is not only tied to physicality but also defensive pressure, contested shots at the rim, and turnovers. Before Bickerstaff took over the Pistons, they had a defensive rating of 118 in 2023-24. That was 25th in the league. In his first season at the helm, the Pistons had a rating of 112.5, which was good for 10th-best, and last season, they had a defensive rating of 108.9, second-best. Last season, they also averaged 10.4 steals and 6.4 blocks per game, both of which were best in the league. The season before Bickerstaff arrived, the Pistons were dead last in the NBA with 6.5 steals per game and were 20th in the league with 4.7 blocks per game. While some of that improvement can be tied to personnel, many of the key players on the Pistons were in Detroit before Bickerstaff arrived. Cade Cunningham played three seasons in Detroit before Bickerstaff was hired, but he had never made an All-Star Game and had only averaged a steal per game in one of those seasons. Jalen Duren played two seasons in Detroit prior to Bickerstaff being hired, and Ausar Thompson played one. Their evolution as players can be attributed to increased experience and maturity, but it would be foolish not to give some credit to the identity created in Detroit over the last two seasons. “We play Pistons basketball. It doesn't matter who our opponent is or what the rest of the league is doing," explained Bickerstaff. "We're built a certain way, and if we're trying to change because of what everybody else is doing, we're not going to be as good at it, and we're not going to be as true to ourselves. That's the most important thing. All the changes that have happened [in the Eastern Conference], your identity matters, right? Your style of play is second to your identity, and if you're playing true to your identity every single night, that gives you an advantage when you're playing against teams that are trying to figure out who they are or what they do. So our aim is just to be who we are, right? We play Pistons ball every single night.” Having that built-in identity has also made it easier for new players to adapt to what the Pistons are doing. Guys like Paul Reed, Duncan Robinson, John Collins, and Isaiah Joe can become integrated into the team quickly because the identity is so clear-cut. "I think the way the league is going to be is you're going to have some overhaul with a lot of teams just because of the new salary structure and all that stuff," said Bickerstaff. "I think the more simple you can make it, the more quickly you can get guys to buy into it, and the more you get to maintain your identity by seeking new players that kind of fit, and I think that's what we've been able to do. Give the front office a ton of credit; they found guys that fit our identity and the way that we play." The way the Pistons play has worked too. Last season, they finished the regular season 60-22 and were the top seed in the Eastern Conference playoffs. The season before, they were 44-38 and finished as the 6th seed. That was after a season in which they were 14-68 and were the worst team in the Eastern Conference. It was a pretty quick rise to title contention, and much of that has to do with style of play. Yet, "Pistons basketball" also does come with some negatives. Since Bickerstaff took over and instilled his more physical brand of basketball, the Pistons have been among the leaders in the NBA in fouls. In his first season, they committed 20.7 fouls per game, the fourth-most in the league. Last season, they led the league with 22 fouls per game. Now, the Pistons also had the third-most fouls per game the season before Bickerstaff was hired, so this is not strictly an issue tied to his style of play, but it is something he has embraced as a head coach. "We're physical within the rules and have gotten really good at it," he declared after the loss to the Knicks. "We've been one of the top defenses over the past two, three years, whatever it's been. We play a certain style, and fans want to see the style that we play. That's what Detroit wants, and that's what our fan base enjoys about this team, so we'll continue to do what we do." The issue the Pistons will need to reconcile with is that their approach may make it harder to reach their ultimate goal of an NBA title. While the league has continued to assert that games are not called differently in the regular season and the playoffs, recent data has shown that games are officiated much tighter in the postseason. Last season, referees called 11% more fouls per game in the playoffs than in the regular season . While that was one of the largest gaps in league history, and only the sixth time in 60 years that the foul gap between regular season and playoffs topped 10%, the NBA has had an increase in foul calls from the regular season to the playoffs 66 times in its 80-year history. The 2025 season saw the biggest gap between regular-season and playoff fouls in over a decade, and 2026 increased that gap. It's also not a gap that the league is running from. In that ESPN article linked above, NBA senior vice president of referee development and training Monty McCutchen said, "It would be very difficult on our players, on our coaches, most certainly on our referees, if the intensity of a seven-game series that we see in the playoffs exhibited itself over 82 games. "NBA playoff basketball is one of the great spectacles of all sports in my opinion. You get the combination of the passion and strength of our players and coaching staffs in tight spaces over a seven-game series. And I think that that absolutely makes for a different game." Even though the NBA acknowledges that playoff basketball is inherently more physical, it seems likely to still use the whistle more often in the postseason. That was one bugaboo for the Pistons last season. While they allowed 27.2 free throws per game to their opponents in the regular season, they allowed 29.2 per game in the postseason. Cleveland averaged 30 free throws per game in their victory over the Pistons in the Eastern Conference Semi-Finals. Those may seem like minor disparities, but every point matters in the postseason, especially since the pace is slower, which means fewer offensive possessions and shot attempts per game. The bigger issue at play may be that Detroit's edge in physicality, which helps so much in the regular season, becomes less pronounced in the playoffs. Playoff games are slower and more physical by nature. Most of the teams that make the playoffs are strong defensive teams. Scoring overall in last year's playoffs fell, with teams averaging about 117.8 points in the regular season and just 105 points in the postseason. Sportico’s 2025 study of NBA Playoff basketball suggested that the slower pace and stingier defense in the playoffs make it "more difficult for teams to generate open shots close to the basket." As a result, "paint touches have consistently declined in the postseason throughout the player tracking era since 2014." That means offenses have to settle for more three-pointers, but three-point percentage decreases in the postseason: "Of the 224 playoff squads since 2010, excluding those in the 2020 playoff bubble, nearly three-quarters (72%) shot worse from behind the 3-point line during the postseason than the regular season." That means teams that take more three-pointers give themselves more opportunity to overcome the worse shooting. The Sportico report also mentioned that the more aggressive postseason defense "limits transition opportunities and shots around the basket while forcing teams out of their offensive sets." That's detrimental to a Pistons team that creates so much offense through their defense creating transition opportunities. Last season, they were 1st in turnovers forced, 2nd in fast break points per game, and 2nd in points in the paint per game in the regular season. However, their offense really struggled in the paint against the interior defense of Jarrett Allen and Evan Mobley in that loss to the Cavaliers. So even if the physical nature of the Pistons' defense hasn't been detrimental to their playoff success in the past two years, their physical, transition-oriented offense has made it harder for them to score points in the postseason. In order for them to make a deep run in the playoffs, they will need to modify a little bit of what "Pistons basketball" means on the offensive end. So far, through four games of the 2026-27 NBA season, we are seeing them start to make a few of those changes. While the offensive rebounding and strong interior offense have remained, the Pistons appear to be playing a little bit faster and spacing the court better than they did last season. Last year, they were 17th in the NBA in three-point shooting at 35.6% on 30.9 attempts per game, and 28% of their points came on threes, which was 29th in the NBA. This season, Detroit is 9th in the NBA in three-point shooting at 37.6% on 37.3 attempts per game, and 37.2% of Detroit’s points have come off threes, which is 10th-most in the NBA. That's a major difference. This season, the threes the Pistons are getting are also based mostly on pace and ball movement. Through four games, 29 of the Pistons’ 37.3 three-point attempts per game are on catch-and-shoot chances. That’s the 9th most in the league, and they have a 56.2% effective field goal rate on those attempts, which is 11th-best in the NBA. Last season, just 22.5 of their 31 attempts per game were on catch-and-shoot threes, 26th-most in the league. A big part of that increase has been Coach Bickerstaff changing how he uses sharpshooter Duncan Robinson, using him more as an on-ball screener to free him up to get open looks when defenders help on the screen. Using Duncan as a screener “just puts defenses in tough decisions,” explained Bickerstaff. “Especially when you get him in some of those rip screens for John [Collins], who has the lob threat ability. Do you want to switch a smaller guy onto him? Do you have to bump him? Then Duncan's so intelligent. He does a great job of reading those screens and what the defenders do, and he's a step ahead of them. He knows when to slip out, he knows when to set it, he knows what route to take to get to the next screen quicker. So all those things just make it easier for him to create those opportunities and put defenses in tough situations.” Collins himself is also a 37% shooter from deep in his career, and Isaiah Joe, who was acquired from the Thunder this offseason, has shot 40.5% from beyond the arc in his seven seasons. All of that seems to be an acknowledgement that, offensively, "Pistons basketball" needs to adapt. The physicality and aggression can remain, but when teams rise up to meet that level of play in the postseason, Detroit needs to have another wrinkle to throw at teams if they want to reach the ultimate prize. We're only four games into the new season, but this version of "Pistons basketball" may just be the most playoff-friendly version we've seen in years.

stories.detailText: Indiana Pacers All-Star point guard Tyrese Haliburton has suffered a mild left hamstring strain and will miss at least two weeks recovering, head coach Rick Carlisle said on Wednesday afternoon. Haliburton is being considered week-to-week, though an update isn’t expected for at least two weeks. A clearer timeline for his return is not yet known. Haliburton has had issues with that left hamstring before. He strained it while slipping on a drive to the basket during a game against the Boston Celtics in January of 2024 , costing him 10 games; he'd manage that injury for the rest of the regular season, before re-aggravating it during the Eastern Conference finals against Boston four months later. The following season, he left a January contest against the Cleveland Cavaliers early with left hamstring tightness , and missed the Pacers' following game, too. The 26-year-old point guard missed all of the 2025-26 regular season after rupturing his right Achilles tendon during Game 7 of the 2025 NBA Finals . He played in the Pacers' first four games of the 2026-27 campaign, and is averaging 21.8 points, 9.5 assists and 4.5 rebounds in 33 minutes per game, shooting 51.6% from the field, 37% from 3-point range and 86.7% from the free-throw line. After an emotional return to the lineup in a win over the New Orleans Pelicans, Haliburton appeared to be fully back in the fold for a Pacers team that had looked all but bereft without him last season. He put up 20-and-10 double-doubles in two of his first three games back, leading Indiana to wins in New Orleans and Brooklyn. Haliburton pressed to play in the second half of Indiana's first back-to-back set of the season, when the Pacers traveled to his native Wisconsin to take on the rival Milwaukee Bucks. He logged a season-high 35 minutes in the Pacers' 110-102 loss ; he was seen wearing a heating pad on his left hamstring while seated on the Indiana bench. After the back-to-back, Haliburton had been listed as questionable for the Pacers' Wednesday game against the Philadelphia 76ers with left hamstring tightness/soreness — one of eight Indiana players on the injury report , and the third dealing specifically with a hamstring ailment, joining Aaron Nesmith and T.J. McConnell, who has yet to play this season. The Pacers will be without Haliburton, McConnell, starting center Ivica Zubac (left ankle sprain) and reserve wings Ben Sheppard and Johnny Furphy against Philly on Wednesday. Guard Andrew Nembhard (neck soreness) is also listed as questionable. Amid this spate of early-season injuries, Indiana has opened the season 2-2, with the NBA's No. 16 offense and No. 14 defense . The Pacers have outscored opponents by four points per 100 non-garbage-time possessions with Haliburton on the floor , and have been outscored by 7.4 points-per-100 with him off it — the largest on-off swing on the team . Some of that stems from the other absences up and down the roster, most notably to backup point guard McConnell; some of it, though, highlights just how central and critical a figure Haliburton is to Indiana's chances of success. The early woes call to mind the raft of injuries that Indiana suffered at the start of the 2024-25 season, contributing to a rocky start that saw Haliburton and Co. sitting at 10-15 in early December. Once the Pacers got healthy, though, they took off, blossoming into one of the NBA's best teams on both ends of the floor and eventually making it all the way to Game 7 of the Finals. This year's model will hope to follow in its predecessors' footsteps, with Pascal Siakam and the reserve corps holding down the fort until the ailing bodies — and specifically Haliburton's — can get back to full strength and full speed. Haliburton is the latest in a string of stars to suffer injuries in the early days of this NBA season, joining the likes of Anthony Edwards , Jaren Jackson Jr. , Kawhi Leonard , Jalen Williams , Jalen Duren and Paolo Banchero .

stories.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘He’s just a different person’
stories.summary: Just when I thought we were hunting for the No. 1 overall pick in the 2027 NBA Draft… …Mike Brown and the lads decided to get their excrement together and remind us the Knicks are actually a title contender. Here’s the latest before we turn the page quickly to this evening’s affair against the Chicago […]
stories.detailText: NEW YORK, NEW YORK - OCTOBER 25: Josh Hart #3 of the New York Knicks warms up before the game against the Orlando Magic at Madison Square Garden on October 25, 2026 in New York City.
