stories.title: Carlton Davis ready to make return vs. Dolphins
stories.summary: The Patriots starting cornerback has missed the last three games.
stories.detailText: New England Patriots cornerback Carlton Davis III is ready to make his return to the field this Sunday against the Miami Dolphins. Davis initially injured his neck in the season opener against Seattle and missed the Week 2 contest against the Steelers. He came back for the following two weeks before missing the Patriots’ last three games. The cornerback feels his initial return was too soon, but he is now ready to go. “Just day in, day out, trying to look for ways to get better,” Davis said. “Not trying to rush the process, but really trying to be efficient, recovering, and getting back out there, being a guy that my team can depend on. “I think the worst is just sitting on the sideline, watching plays being made or being a bystander. Last year, I played in every game. This year I was looking to do the same, and it’s a bit disappointing to not be able to do that. But I’m back here and ready to go.” The Patriots secondary has not been at full force since Week 1 in Seattle. In addition to Davis, New England has played without safety Craig Woodson for one game and cornerback Christian Gonzalez for two. Now healthy, the group is excited to be back on the field together. “It’s going to be great having all the guys back, being at full power and being able to go out there and feed off each other and make plays together,” Davis said. Gonzalez, who battled an illness last week, shared he was feeling better on Wednesday. He was excited as well to get his fellow cornerback back. “It’s everything. CD is a great vet, somebody that I lean on a lot, able to talk to, pick his mind about certain things,” Gonzalez said. “He’s seen a lot of ball, so just having him back out there is amazing. So, excited to get all of us back. I think this is the first game since the first week it’s going to be all of us out there. So excited for that to get back on the field with all that.”

stories.title: Badgers star considered a potential Day 2 draft pick as stellar season continues
stories.summary: Wisconsin could have its first Day 2 pick since 2023.
stories.detailText: Alessio Milivojevic #11 of the Michigan State Spartans throws a pass while pressured by Sebastian Cheeks #15 of the Wisconsin Badgers at Camp Randall Stadium in Madison, Wisconsin, on October 3, 2026. (Photo by Ross Harried/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images Wisconsin Badgers star edge rusher Sebastian Cheeks has been one of the best pass rushers in the country this season. So far, he ranks second among Power 4 edge rushers with 34 pressures, despite playing one less game than the majority of the leaderboard. Cheeks is coming off a game against USC where he had six pressures, 2.5 sacks, and four defensive stops, wreaking havoc on star quarterback Jayden Maiava. Cheeks’s 34 pressures are already more than what he had all of last season, and he’s been a vital cog in an elite Badgers defensive unit this season. After starting the year being considered as an undrafted prospect, Cheeks’s stock has really started to rise, and he could even be a Day 2 pick in the 2027 NFL Draft. In his weekly notes, ESPN’s Mel Kiper praised Cheeks and his ability to get to the quarterback, noting he currently has a Round 3 or Round 4 grade on the Badgers edge rusher. “I love how Wisconsin edge rusher Sebastian Cheeks varies his path to the quarterback,” Kiper wrote. “He can get home on the inside or outside with explosion, and he always has a secondary move ready to go. We saw that against USC, with 2.5 sacks. And at 6-3 and 243 pounds, he plays with more power than you might think — he can drive offensive tackles back with his bull rush. “His motor never stops. Cheeks will make plays against the run, too, but he needs to add more weight to his frame to really take another step there. Cheeks shows sustained intensity and is a consistent player, and I have him in Round 3 or Round 4.” Cheeks earned the Big Ten Defensive Player of the Week honor this past week after his strong performance against USC, marking the first time a Badger earned the award since Darryl Peterson against Illinois last November. Wisconsin hasn’t had a player taken on Day 2 of the NFL Draft since center Joe Tippmann went to New York Jets and defensive tackle Keeanu Benton went to the Pittsburgh Steelers in the second round of the 2023 NFL Draft. That was also the year that edge rusher Nick Herbig was drafted by the Steelers, which happened in the fourth round. Herbig was the last Badgers edge rusher to be drafted, and he’s enjoyed a nice NFL career, earning a four-year, $100 million contract this past offseason. Cheeks and the Badgers defense will look to finish the season strong, as Wisconsin looks to make a late-season push in the Big Ten after starting the season 5-2 and 3-1 in conference play. If he does so, his draft stock should continue to rise after an impressive start to the season.

stories.title: Chiefs coach defends decision to sign kicker Tucker
stories.summary: Kansas City Chiefs head coach Andy Reid defends the franchise's decision to sign Justin Tucker to its practice squad, stating the kicker has "done his suspension".
stories.detailText: Justin Tucker was signed by the Ravens as an undrafted free agent in 2012 [Getty Images] Kansas City Chiefs head coach Andy Reid has defended the decision to sign Justin Tucker to their practice squad, stating the kicker has "done his suspension". Tucker, one of the most accurate kickers in NFL history, was last year accused of sexual misconduct by 16 massage therapists in the Baltimore area during the 2010s. The 36-year-old - who won Super Bowl XLVII with the Baltimore Ravens - has consistently denied the allegations and never faced criminal charges. Following an investigation, Tucker received a 10-game suspension from the NFL for violating the league's personal conduct policy. He was released by Baltimore in May 2025 in what they described as a "football decision" following declining form. Having served the ban last season, Tucker is immediately available for selection. Reid said in a news conference on Wednesday: "He's done his suspension, taking care of that business there. I'll leave it at that. "We try to do our homework the best way we possibly can and talk to a lot of people, make sure things are okay." Pressed on what he meant by "homework", Reid added: "I'm not going to get into all that. To bring him here, I did some homework. "He's here and he's on the practice squad, so we roll with it." Tucker, a five-time All-Pro, is second in NFL history in field-goal percentage, making 89.1% of his attempts across 13 seasons, but endured the worst season of his career in 2024, kicking just 73.3% of his field-goal attempts. The Chiefs made their move for him following a run of poor form by Harrison Butker, who has been the team's kicker since 2017 and has the fifth-best accuracy (87.3%) in NFL history. However, the 31-year-old has missed five of his 16 field-goal attempts this season, including two from three in a 20-3 defeat by the Seattle Seahawks on Saturday. stories.title: Lions, Vikings Week 8 injury report: Jahmyr Gibbs sits with shoulder injury

stories.detailText: Oct 11, 2026; Glendale, Arizona, USA; Detroit Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs (0) against the Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Detroit Lions (4-2) will host the Minnesota Vikings (6-0) in Week 8, and both teams were on the practice field on Wednesday, preparing for their Sunday afternoon battle at Ford Field. The Lions have only a few injured players this week—Amon Ra St. Brown and Ennis Rakestraw were injured in Week 7—but they also elected to rest several injured players on Wednesday; most, if not all, are expected to return to practice this week. “We’re going to do a walkthrough and then roll right into practice for a little bit here,” Lions coach Dan Campbell explained at Wednesday’s press conference. “I think those guys (St. Brown and Rakestraw) will be at walkthrough, but I don’t see them out there during the practice portion. I’m going to hold a couple of other guys back just to get them off their feet, but they’ll be at walkthrough.” Additionally, the Lions received terrific news on Wednesday, as All-Pro safety Kerby Joseph is now healthy enough to practice, and the team has started his injury evaluation clock , making him eligible to practice. Let’s take a look at Wednesday’s injury report and get you up to date with what we know. Note: Any changes from the most recent injury report will be bolded . Injured list updates RB Isiah Pacheco (MCL/Back, IR) — expected to be out until December OL Giovanni Manu (Undisclosed, NFI) — eligible to begin practicing at any time OL Ben Bartch (foot, IR) — eligible to begin practicing in Week 10 LB Devin White (forearm, IR) — eligible to begin practicing in Week 10 S Kerby Joseph (Knee, PUP) — Injury evaluation clock started on October 28 S Thomas Harper (Ankle, IR) — eligible to begin practicing at any time After a few hints on social media, Kerby Joseph is officially returning to practice. Here’s coach Campbell on the decision: “We’re going to start Kerby’s clock today. So, he’ll be running around. Start working him in. He’s put in a lot of work; it’s been a long, hard road for Kerby. So, just being able to get back out there with the guys and run around a little bit. But we will kind of progress him as we go, each week here, just to get him back in the flow, the movement, the flow, the pounding, and all of it. But he’s passed every test to this point, and the next thing is to get him running around now. The strength in the knee is good, and the thigh, the quad, and all of that. So it’ll be great to get him back out there with all the guys.” Joseph has 21 days to be evaluated by the team before they need to decide on his status, but they can return him to the active roster at any time. An encouraging sign when combined with Campbell’s optimism on Monday: “It’s not major, he’s got a little ankle here. We feel like, as of right now, he’ll be at practice on Thursday. stories.title: Colts' fire sale can help with impending QB problem, but it won't be easy
stories.summary: The Colts have a lot to figure out in the coming months, and their quarterback problem might be the most concerning element.
stories.detailText: This week, the Indianapolis Colts have traded two of former GM Chris Ballard's biggest acquisitions during his time with the team, Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner. More players soon could be sent packing. What follows is anyone's guess, but the road eventually must lead to where Ballard struggled to: closer to quarterback salvation. The franchise has a lot to figure out in the next six or so months, and only limited resources with which to do so. Head coach Shane Steichen, 2-5 this season and 27-31 overall, could be fighting for his job — and now with less talent at hand. Interim GM Ed Dodds, who replaced the fired Ballard, has a very short window to prove he's the man for the full-time job. And the quarterback problem isn't going away. That's in addition to plugging the various roster holes, which have only increased this week. Doing so without a first-round choice in 2027 only ups the degree of difficulty. The Colts could hit absolute grand slams with their head coach and GM decisions, and they'd still find themselves in a tough QB spot next spring. Let's dive into what the Colts have now, their limitations for upgrading the position and what the most realistic solutions might be. Are any Colts QBs part of the future? Daniel Jones is the starter now, as Steichen has stuck with him in spite of his 2026 struggles, but Jones does not appear to be a long-term solution right now. There was hope after his strong play last season, but Jones has been turning the ball over at an alarming rate coming off an Achilles injury that ended last season. If he's still on the roster next March, Jones would be owed another $10 million guaranteed and a $4 million roster bonus. Keeping him, especially with that kicker, just doesn't equate right now. The Colts drafted Anthony Richardson fourth overall in 2023, but he's taken only about a dozen regular-season snaps since his final start in the 2024 campaign. The way the Colts have acted the past few seasons, they've chalked him up to a sunk cost and merely stashing him in case of emergency. Richardson is a free agent next spring, and it would be a surprise to see him back as well. Riley Leonard is the only realistic option on the roster now to stick around. He had a few intriguing moments last season, including the Week 18 start at Houston, that kept him with the Colts. If Jones keeps stumbling, they could turn to him this season down the stretch. But how solid an asset is Howard? The Colts likely need more game film to decide, but there's a ceiling right now to the former sixth-round pick's potential. Keep in mind that the Colts bypassed Leonard at first last season for signing Philip Rivers, who was four years removed from his last game, before giving him a meaningless-game shot. In short, there's not a whole lot to count on. Expect a largely — and perhaps entirely — new QB room in 2027. Most likely route to finding a 2027 starter Free agency is a very limited route to finding a starting quarterback because few teams will allow high-quality options to simply walk unimpeded in free agency. Sam Darnold situations do occur every few years, but they're not terribly common events all told. Point being: The Colts have to understand that any QB options they might consider as unrestricted free agents almost always come with warts. Deshaun Watson is a perfect example. Even if he plays acceptably well for the remainder of the season with the Browns, signing him as a free agent — yes, he finally hits the market again — comes with a ton of baggage and likely wouldn't inspire the fanbase. Justin Fields isn't on the Darnold spectrum yet, even if he's a highly paid backup with 53 career starts. The same probably applies to the likes of Davis Mills and Jarrett Stidham. 49ers QB Mac Jones could be a starting option for the Colts next season. Cooper Neill via Getty Images The one possibly intriguing option among the free agents to-be is likely the 49ers' Mac Jones. He's started 53 games, has marinated in the 49ers' system for a few years and stepped in readily for an injured Brock Purdy a year ago. The Jones likelihood only increases if the Colts consider any 49ers assistants (Klay Kubiak, perhaps?) as a head-coaching candidate. Otherwise, the Colts would be shopping on some familiar streets with some of the veteran options who'll be available, including Jacoby Brissett, Kirk Cousins and Marcus Mariota. Those aren't bad options if the Colts can pair them with a young QB and sell the veteran on a bridge-QB role for 2027. Can the Colts find QB help in the 2027 draft? This leads us to the other elephant in the room. The 2027 NFL Draft, once pegged as a possibly generational class at quarterback, now looks tepid in some respects. There are some quality prospects in the 2027 mix now, but the class as a whole has not taken off as hoped. The Colts lack their 2027 first-round pick from the Sauce Gardner trade, and even after the Nelson and Buckner trades, they still have only one guaranteed top-64 selection to their names currently. The extra mid-round selections could allow a trade-up situation from high in Round 2, assuming the Colts finish with a losing record, but it still would be a heavier lift to get into the first round. For years, the late first- to early second-round range was a wasteland for quarterbacks, but in the past decade it has produced Lamar Jackson, Jordan Love, Tyler Shough and Jaxson Dart. It has also given us Will Levis and Drew Lock. But on the whole, you'd say any draft range that theoretically produces a better-than-50% ROI has to be considered pretty fertile grounds. Even if next year's class isn't what we had hoped, there still could be some options who project in a similar range. Oregon QB Dante Moore hasn't boosted his draft stock, but that could put him more in play for a team such as the Colts. Icon Sportswire via Getty Images One is Oregon's Dante Moore. He might have been the No. 2 overall pick had he come out a year ago, but Moore's slower start this season and a season-ending concussion have his draft stock hanging in the void a bit. It's possible he could slide and be within range of where the Colts end up picking. Miami's Darian Mensah might be trending toward a first-round landing spot, but that's not guaranteed yet. USC's Jayden Maiava, who is out of eligibility after this season, will be in the upcoming class, and he's played well so far this season; his range has yet to crystallize, but he's another who might not be far out of reach. There could be other candidates, including Notre Dame's C.J. Carr, Missouri's Austin Simmons and Ohio State's Julian Sayin, but all of them will have options to return to school. The wild card might be South Carolina's LaNorris Sellers, but as a very toolsy but also flawed prospect, Sellers might hit a little too optically close to the Richardson mark to be the preferred choice. The answer to our original question is probably a soft "yes." The Colts can find someone with some potential upside, but it might require a mix of luck and aggression come draft time. The outlook at this point is far from dim, but it's also not wholly inspiring. Best guess right now is that the Colts — whoever is running them in three months — will opt to pair a veteran free agent with Leonard and a draft prospect who ranks somewhere between QB3 and QB6 on most consensus boards. Is it an exciting plan? Maybe not, but given the Colts' situation and the deep rebuild they're facing, it probably could be worse.

stories.title: Winless Chargers sticking with Mike McDaniel as offensive playcaller
stories.summary: Embattled offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel will continue as the Chargers' playcaller, coach Jim Harbaugh announced Wednesday.
stories.detailText: Embattled offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel will continue as the Los Angeles Chargers ' playcaller, coach Jim Harbaugh announced Wednesday. "We're very confident in Mike and his talent, his work ethic and his ability," Harbaugh told reporters, according to The Athletic . "We continue to be." Harbaugh made the decision after the organization's self-scouting over their bye week. "I feel like every stone, any part that we could look to better, that's the way we responded," Harbaugh said. Before their Week 7 bye, the Chargers scored a season-low six points in a Week 6 loss to the Kansas City Chiefs . The Chargers managed just 259 total yards and lowered their league-worst points-per-game average to 15.0 in the 22-6 loss, which dropped them to 0-6 on the season. They are the league's last winless team this season. McDaniel, who was fired in January after four seasons as the head coach of the Miami Dolphins , joined the Chargers this offseason to jump-start a Chargers offense that had scored only one touchdown over two playoff losses under Harbaugh. McDaniel said his goal was to help Justin Herbert , whom he called as talented a quarterback as he had ever been around, "own" the position. That process began with Herbert changing his shotgun stance over the offseason, moving his left foot in front of his right. It's a change McDaniel has made with other quarterbacks, most recently with Tua Tagovailoa in Miami, who had his only Pro Bowl in Year 2 under McDaniel. Herbert took days off from throwing at practice, instead practicing footwork while going through a throwing motion with a green water ball while McDaniel watched closely. Instead, the Chargers' offense and Herbert have never looked worse. He has thrown interceptions directly to defenders: to Buffalo Bills safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson in Week 3, then two picks to Seattle Seahawks linebacker Drake Thomas and linebacker Ernest Jones IV in Week 4. He has looked like a shell of the player many consider to be among the league's top quarterbacks, as the Chargers have piled up losses. Herbert is tied for the NFL lead with eight interceptions this season. McDaniel arrived in Los Angeles as one of the most respected offensive playcallers in the NFL, responsible for some of the greatest offenses in league history. In 2023, his Dolphins beat the Denver Broncos 70-20 with 700-plus yards of offense in a game and tied the record for points scored in a game. ESPN's Kris Rhim contributed to this report.

stories.title: Packers and Panthers trying to bounce back as they face off at Lambeau Field
stories.summary: — A pair of ticked-off teams will square off when the Green Bay Packers face the Carolina Panthers on Thursday night.
stories.detailText: GREEN BAY, Wis. -- — A pair of ticked-off teams will square off when the Green Bay Packers face the Carolina Panthers on Thursday night. The Packers (4-3) are angry over a 20-17 loss at Detroit in which they got penalized seven times in the second half, leading to postgame critiques of the officiating. Carolina (3-3) is mad at itself after getting blown out 43-13 at home by the Tampa Bay Buccaneers . So neither team should have any trouble finding motivation. “Just for us, this is the next game, this is the next championship opportunity,” Panthers coach Dave Canales said. "But I’m also fully aware there’s a human element involved. And for us, coming off of that loss in the fashion that we lost, for the Packers, a really tough loss for them as well, there’s something that burns inside of you as a competitor. And in me, in our players, certainly in the Green Bay Packers’ locker room, too.” Green Bay comes into this one with injury issues on its offensive line after losing starting center Sean Rhyan and backup Jacob Monk in the Lions game. Right guard Travis Glover won't play Thursday due to a knee issue. This continues a season-long problem for the Packers, who have had different starting offensive line combinations in each of their first four games. “It’s different, but at the end of the day, we still trust the guys,” said Packers running back Josh Jacobs , who made his season debut Sunday after spending Green Bay’s first six games on the commissioner’s exempt list. “I know for the running backs and the O-line, we met together just with us. We went over the film and stuff like that, and the standard is still the standard regardless of who’s in there.” Green Bay also will be missing linebacker Zaire Franklin (shin) for a second straight game. Carolina has ruled out cornerback Akayleb Evans (triceps/knee), guard Damien Lewis (knee), outside linebacker Jaelan Phillips (hamstring) and offensive lineman Torricelli Simpkins (ankle). This represents a rematch of a game the Panthers won 16-13 at Lambeau Field last year. “We know that doesn’t entitle us to anything," Panthers quarterback Bryce Young said. "It’s a new year, new season, new guys on both sides of the ball. For us, that’s not something we’re pulling from or referencing.” The Packers lost to Carolina last season in part because of their inability to capitalize when they got inside the opponent’s 35-yard line, a problem that also proved costly Sunday at Detroit. Carolina would love to see its defense show that same kind of stinginess Thursday after allowing the Buccaneers to run wild. “I’m sure we have a very motivated team coming in here, and certainly one that we know is dangerous,” Packers coach Matt LaFleur said. “Shoot, they came in here last year and beat us. But I think we’re motivated as well, and we’ve got to bounce back.” Need to know Carolina (3-3) at Green Bay (4-3) When/where to watch: Thursday, 8:15 p.m. EDT, Prime Video Latest odds: Packers by 3½ Against the spread: Panthers 3-3; Packers 3-3-1 Last week: Panthers lost 43-13 at home to Tampa Bay Buccaneers; Packers lost 20-17 at Detroit Last meeting: Panthers beat Packers 16-13 on Nov. 2, 2025, in Green Bay, Wisconsin Series record: Packers lead 12-7 Matchup to watch Packers running game vs. Panthers run defense. This matchup features each team’s biggest weakness. Green Bay is running for an NFL-low 59.9 yards per game, while Carolina is allowing a league-high 153.2 yards rushing per game. Carolina allowed Tampa Bay to rush for 258 yards on Sunday in what defensive tackle Derrick Brown called an “embarrassing performance.” Green Bay hasn’t run for more than 86 yards in any game this season. Stats and stuff — Panthers QB Bryce Young ranks second in the NFL in passing yards per game (285.3). He has thrown a touchdown pass in eight straight games, including playoffs. — Carolina ranks fifth in the NFL in points per game (26.5) and yards per game (381.3). — The Panthers have an NFL-leading nine receivers with at least one 25-yard catch this season. — Panthers RB Chuba Hubbard rushed for at least 120 yards in two straight games before being limited to 33 yard on seven carries against the Bucs. — Carolina has a league-high 79.2 penalty yards per game. Green Bay is second with 78 penalty yards per game. The Packers have a league-high 9.3 penalties per game. — The Packers have a league-high 33 plays from scrimmage of at least 20 yards. Packers QB Jordan Love has a league-leading 30 completions of at least 20 yards. — Packers WR Christian Watson has six touchdown catches to rank second in the NFL. Seattle’s Jaxon Smith-Njigba has eight. — Packers K Trey Smack missed field goal attempts from 26 and 35 yards in the loss to the Lions. The 35-yarder was deflected. — See AP’s full NFL coverage here

stories.title: Explosive play rates: A tale of two sides for the 49ers
stories.summary: Top five on both sides of the ball?
stories.detailText: (Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images) | Getty Images As the San Francisco 49ers enjoy their bye week and evaluate their season through seven weeks, the front office has been busy making calls around the NFL. DeForest Buckner is back, and an educated guess would be that the organization isn’t done making moves. With a 6-1 record, even after a frustrating loss to Atlanta, the 49ers couldn’t ask for a better start, especially with wins over tough defenses like Denver and Seattle. How have the 49ers done it? Explosive play rates on both sides of the ball. In this case, an explosive play is a run over ten-plus yards and a pass over 20-plus yards. The 49ers offense is top five in explosive play rate at 9.5%. The top four offenses in explosive play rates are Buffalo, Miami (what the hell?), Kansas City, and Baltimore. A closer look shows the 49ers’ rushing attack at number four with 14.1% and a passing attack at 5.6%, which is good for 11th in the league. With Mike Evans returning and others, that number should be trending upwards. What about defensively? The 49ers defense is first in explosive play rate allowed at 3.2%. With the best rushing defense number of 2.9% and the fifth-best passing defense at 3.5%, the 49ers defense will see a decrease in those numbers with Buckner and Nick Bosa playing next week and for the rest of the season, hopefully. Last week, the 49ers defense struggled to generate pass rush, but they weren’t hit over the top against Atlanta. Unfortunately, the deep Cover 3 zones run by Raheem Morris, paired with the struggling pass rush, allowed Michael Penix and the Falcons offense to convert underneath methodically. The 49ers’ run defense did a great job bottling up one of the most explosive backs in the NFL, Bijan Robinson. The NFL as a whole has converted to a two-man safety shell look, which is designed to limit explosive plays and keep everything in front of second- and third-level defenders. If the 49ers continue at this pace, they will be just fine. However, it is fair to expect an increase in explosives on offense and a decrease on defense. That is how the 49ers have a 6-1 record.

stories.title: Eagles star Saquon Barkley says he was forced to divest Polymarket equity stake
stories.summary: Eagles star Saquon Barkley said he was forced to divest his equity stake in Polymarket to comply with NFL rules.
stories.detailText: PHILADELPHIA -- Philadelphia Eagles running back Saquon Barkley said he was forced to divest his equity stake in Polymarket to comply with NFL rules that prohibit players from investing in gambling or prediction-market companies. Barkley told Front Office Sports that the league relays to players before each season what they can and can't endorse and invest in, and that being involved with prediction markets is no longer allowed. "I was in it before, but no bueno," he told Front Office Sports, which posted its report about Barkley on Wednesday. According to Front Office Sports, an NFL Players Association spokesperson said earlier in the year that the league "views prediction markets as gambling entities, so players are not allowed to be an endorser or brand ambassador for a company like Kalshi or Polymarket under the gambling policy." Barkley has been active in the investment space. He has invested upwards of $500,000 in startup companies like Anthropic, Anduril, Ramp, Cognition, Neuralink, Strike, and Polymarket, according to a 2025 report by The Profile. The NFL's stance on prediction market partnerships appears to differ from other sports. The NBA, Major League Baseball, NHL and MLS all have deals with either Kalshi, Polymarket or both. The NFL asked the U.S. Supreme Court earlier this month to review whether prediction markets' sports-event contracts, which mimic traditional sports betting, fall under the purview of state gambling regulators. A league source told ESPN's David Purdum that the NFL's primary desire is for the court to provide clarity on the issue quickly, adding that the league would accept a federal framework if it provided the same regulatory approach as states.

Enter Kirk Herbstreit, who seems to think his perpetual canine shield will keep him from being scrutinized as aggressively as he should be. Last month, Herbstreit addressed the intense (and justified) criticism of ESPN's overt support for the Protect College Sports Act by pointing out that he's decidedly not a political person. “ I don’t really get into politics ," Herbstreit said the Friday after Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Tex.) was loudly booed during an extended infomercial for the PCSA during College GameDay . "It’s just not — I’m kind of an independent guy, right down the middle of the fairway. I’m for America, so whoever helps us as a country, I’m for. Whether it’s somebody on the left, somebody on the right, so I don’t really follow it. I don’t know anything about his political views. I don’t know what he’s for or against. I care about football, my family, and my faith, and my country. Those are things I love." He also loves, apparently, to make time in his otherwise non-stop in-season schedule to appear at political action committee fundraising events. Via David Covucci of FOIABall , Herbstreit served as the keynote speaker at a major Business Council of Alabama function on October 21 — the night before he called the Patriots-Bears game in Chicago. The goal of the event was to raise money for BCA’s political action committee, Progress PAC. “This cornerstone Progress PAC fundraising event commences with VIP gatherings and concludes with dinner and dialogue from a notable guest," the group's website explained, per Covucci. "This important component of Campaign 2026 provides the resources needed to support the election of pro-business candidates across the state.” In political circles, "pro-business" is code for "conservative." And, as Covucci notes, BCA endorsed 108 candidates in Alabama races. Of them, 82 are Republican. Of the 26 Democrats it has endorsed, 20 are running unopposed. The day after the event, BCA funneled $155,000 to the campaign of Republican Senator Tommy Tuberville. Look, Herbstreit can speak at any political event he wants. That's not the issue. The issue is that he responded to the blatant effort by ESPN to boost the PCSA by saying, essentially, "I don't know nothing about no politics." Whatever the specific context, bullshit smells the same in all of them. Even if Herbstreit thinks that taking his dog everywhere he goes will make people feel less inclined to call him out for it.

stories.title: Is it time to start the conversation about benching Cardinals QB Brissett?
stories.summary: A roller coaster of a season
stories.detailText: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - OCTOBER 11: Jacoby Brissett #7 of the Arizona Cardinals reacts after his team was defeated by the Detroit Lions at State Farm Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images It appears that the 2026 version of the Arizona Cardinals is just the version of the team in 2025. Maybe the new boss is just like the old boss. At this rate, something needs to change. Yes, the Cardinals are 2-5-0. But 10 games remain. Is this team headed down the rabbit hole to another double-digit-loss season? Or can they rebound? RELATED: WHEN SHOULD THE CARDINALS START THE CARSON BECK ERA? Arizona has a new offense, but geez, averaging 20.3 points a game is concerning. This side of the ball will drive up and down the field all game, then when they arrive in the Red Zone, the wheels come off, and the offense does not finish. Correct that statement: the offense rarely finishes. The offensive problems with this offense begin with one guy: QB Jacoby Brissett. It’s a sad, sad situation. His all-time starting record? 22-50-0. His starting record while with Arizona? 3-16-0. This new Mike LaFleur offense is ranked #19 overall in the league. They are #18 in total passing yards (1,607), #1 in attempts (283), #2 in completions (184), #13 in pass completion percentage (65.0%), #16 in touchdown passes (10), #23 in fewest interceptions thrown (6), #28 in passing plays of 20+ yards (13), dead last in passing plays of 40+ yards (0), and have given up the 16 th most sacks (15). Where are the explosive plays? Long plays just aren’t a thing with Arizona. They are the only club that hasn’t had a passing play go further than 40 yards, and look at the plays of 20-plus yardage. Just 13? In seven games? The Cardinals boast the league’s best tight end in Trey McBride, and have several dynamic pass catchers in Michael Wilson, Kendrick Bourne, and rookie Reggie Virgil. The offensive line is holding its own despite losing LT Paris Johnson and each week having to Band-Aid who is healthy and who is injured. In the past, Brissett was known for having huge games. He has 10 career 300-yard passing days and one in which he eclipsed 400 yards in the loss to the San Francisco 49ers last year in late November (452). But none of that is happening this year. In the Week 2 loss to the Seattle Seahawks, Brissett had a mere 95 passing yards. 166 in the loss to the New York Football Giants in Week 4. The issue is that Brissett is having to throw a lot in every contest. The average for a quarterback is 28 attempts. This year, Brissett has thrown 37, 28, 52, 35, 47, 35, and 48 attempts. What that means is that the Cardinals aren’t generating much of a running game, so their quarterback has to air it out for much of the contest. That is not sustainable. When the opposing defense realizes that Arizona can’t run, they stop looking for the run and blast off the snap every time, which gives them a distinct advantage. Should this offense sit Brissett? Statistically, his completion percentage is strong. He threw for 73.0% and 73.1% in two games, and in the 60s for four more. That is really a good sign. Any quarterback who can throw for a 65% completion ratio in any game has done his job. These are dream stats for any signalcaller. The main issue with Brissett at the helm is the offense’s inability to get into the end zone. The Cardinals can move the ball up and down the field for much of the game, but as soon as they cross the 20-yard line, it is like time stands still. Here's the story of the season so far: Arizona Cardinals are dead last in red zone efficiency (42.86%). Arizona Cardinals are dead last in points per game allowed (29.7). — Johnny Venerable (@JohnnyVenerable) October 26, 2026 Currently, Arizona is ranked dead last in Red Zone efficiency at 44%. Good teams, such as the San Francisco 49ers, come in at scoring a touchdown on 87% of their trips. Plainly put, the Niners finish drives, while the Cardinals spit and sputter and end up with three points instead of six. Which is gravy for Arizona kicker Chad Ryland. He is the king of having to come in and kick 23-yard field goals because the offense can’t find a way to get into the end zone. He is ranked #2 in field goal attempts, #3 in converted field goals, and he has converted on 89.5% of his attempts. To show how the offense relies on him to bail them out, he has converted 5 of 5 kicks in the 20–29-yard range, and 5 for 5 in the 30–39-yard range. It’s not like he is banging out a bunch of 50-to 60-yard kicks. Last weekend against the Denver Broncos, the Cardinals were 1-5 in Red Zone appearances. They got down to Denver’s 11, 7, and 23 without scoring a touchdown. Drives of 14 plays and 10 plays. While the Broncos were scoring six points a pop, Arizona was getting half that. The week before, in the 18-16 win over the Los Angeles Rams, Ryland did all the scoring. Brissett guided the offense on drives of 10 plays, 12, 15, and 14. The Cardinals were on the Rams’ 16, 12, 3, 19, 9, before Ryland kicked the 43-yard game-winner with no time remaining. Yet each drive ended up with yet another field goal. In the second quarter, Arizona had a first-and-goal at the eight, and after three plays had not punched it in. What about the 15-play drive that began at their own 25-yard line to start the third quarter, and the offense had a first-and-10 on the Rams’ 23 and could only get to the 19 before trotting out Ryland once again? Or the 14-play drive, as the period was about to expire, that volleyed over into Quarter 4 became a first-and-goal at LA’s eight. Four-yard run to the four-yard line, minus three-yard run, minus two-yard pass, field goal. Before this drive, the Cardinals were up 15-9. A touchdown here with just over nine minutes left in the game would have crippled the Rams. Two things about Brissett: He doesn’t have many picks (6), but he also doesn’t throw many touchdowns (10). Which makes absolutely no sense with having access to an exceptional pass-catching tight end like McBride. Raise your hand if this makes any sense. Here’s an idea: Sit Brissett for a few games. Insert backup Gardner Minshew and see what happens. What is the worst that can happen? The Cardinals will lose? They are doing that anyways. Maybe Minshew has a potion that will help this offense get into the end zone. Because the problem isn’t whether this offense can move the ball – it can. It’s getting into the end zone and collecting three points instead of six. By kicking field goals on the majority of drives, it keeps the other team in the ballgame. There is no extension of the lead – ever. Throw Minshew in there and let’s see if anything different pops out. Then, at some point down the schedule, put rookie Carson Beck in some games and see what Arizona has in him, because they will need to know before next April’s NFL Draft. Kick the tires on Beck and see what he can do in a live regular-season game against defensive starters. If Ryland ends up going to the Pro Bowl this year, the first person he should thank is Brissett. Maybe buy him a nice watch.

teamStories.summary: Kirk Cousins has done everything the Las Vegas Raiders expected of him and more. It’s week 8 and he’s leading the NFL in passing touchdowns with 16. The offense has looked competent and is putting up points, but that isn’t enough for Raiders Nation. What is it that Cousins isn’t doing? By itself, those numbers […]
teamStories.detailText: (Photo by Candice Ward/Getty Images) | Getty Images Kirk Cousins has done everything the Las Vegas Raiders expected of him and more. It’s week 8 and he’s leading the NFL in passing touchdowns with 16. The offense has looked competent and is putting up points, but that isn’t enough for Raiders Nation. What is it that Cousins isn’t doing? By itself, those numbers suggest he’s having one helluva season, which in fact he is. #Raiders coach Klint Kubiak: "Kirk is our starting quarterback. There is no controversy. He is playing at a very high level." — Paul Gutierrez (@PaulHGutierrez) October 26, 2026 Diving into the numbers According to Pro-Football-Reference.com , Cousins’ 60.9% on-target percentage is 27th in the league. Yet, the 151 on-target throws are 9th best. In contrast, the 14.1% bad throw metric is 17th in the league and a razor thin .1% above the league average. However, his 35 bad throws are 7th worst. Plagued by 11 total drops (tied for 4th most) on 4.4% of his throws, 15th most. Once again, Cousins is hanging above the league average (4.2) by a thread. Keeping him yo-yo-ing between good throws more than half the time and an above-average amount of drops. The offensive line is providing 2.0 seconds of pocket time, good enough for 20th in the league. Falling a mere .1 seconds below the league average (2.1). Cousins has put up numbers since returning to head coach Klint Kubiak’s offense. Completing 161 of 257 passes. Out of the 161 completions, 99 have gone to Brock Bowers (who missed the first two games), Ashton Jeanty and Michael Mayer. Wide receivers? Tre Tucker and his 16.3 yards per reception are sixth-best in the league; he has four touchdowns (tied for 4th most), yet only 29 catches on 47 targets. Meanwhile, the rest of the receiving corps are either decoys or just guys getting cardio on the field. Both Jalen Nailor and Cody White have eight receptions each; Jack Bech has five, Malik Benson and Dareke Young each have two. This is one of those plays that’s gonna keep Cousins up late tonight. https://t.co/NheV5C178M pic.twitter.com/CWrZ3H4Hg4 — Ryan McFadden (@ryanmcfadden_) October 26, 2026 While half of Cousins’ passing touchdowns (7) have gone to Tucker (4), Bech (1) and Cody White (3) it really seems as though wide receivers are not being used enough. The real question on the table is Cousin’s arm strength enough to feed his wideouts successfully? The consensus is no. For four straight weeks, defenses have blitzed him in obvious passing downs, forcing him to make off-platform throws and restricting his ability to scan the entire field. Here’s the catch-22: Cousins has been missing open receivers; in fact, due to a declining amount of pocket time, he is foregoing his progressions and locking in on his receivers between the hashes. Staring down receivers has caused them to take big hits, leading to some of those drops and as weeks progress, defenders are getting closer and closer to the football. Help Kirk help the Raiders Playing without a running game is incredibly hard to do. Possessing the escape speed of a three-legged turtle practically makes you a sitting duck. Furthermore, not having enough pocket time for receivers to beat press coverage and get open is a damning trifecta, but Cousins overcame it for as long as he could. Cousins has only 5 interceptions this season and one of them was because his receiver slipped and fell on the route. But there have been many close calls; defensive coordinators have studied his tendencies, finding ways to neutralize him while the game is still competitive. Has he missed throws? Yes. Has he missed reads? Yes. Another one of those missed opportunities in the second quarter that Cousins probably wished he had back. He had Tucker opened under neath. https://t.co/A7LsdpxDGi pic.twitter.com/8t0VYg93Lr — Ryan McFadden (@ryanmcfadden_) October 26, 2026 Is Fernando Mendoza going to be able to come in and play at the level Cousins has been playing at or better? Probably not. He is more physically talented; he may even be versed in the terminology and know how to get in and out of plays. Can Mendoza play and process information faster than Cousins? My money is on no, despite having otherworldly success in a play action and run-pass-option type system in Indiana under Curt Cignetti, 15+ years of experience is only gained one way. As Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak said in his press conference on Monday, “Fernando is going to play football. We have a plan. We don’t have a timeline for that. Kirk is playing well, and we’re in the hunt.” So until the Raiders are out of it, Cousins can’t go, or come high water Cap’n Kirk is here to stay.

2026 NFL trade deadline: Ranking the top 25 candidates to move, plus team fits
teamStories.summary: Could the Colts listen on Jonathan Taylor? Would Josh Sweat help a contender's defense? We stacked the top players who might move before the Nov. 10 deadline.
teamStories.detailText: We're less than two weeks away from the 2026 NFL trade deadline (Tuesday, Nov. 10, at 4 p.m. ET). Which players could potentially be available? And which trade candidates could make the biggest impact with new teams if they do get moved? NFL analyst Matt Bowen and national NFL reporter Jeremy Fowler worked together to build a comprehensive list of the top 25 possible trade candidates. To be clear: Players are ranked here by the potential value they'd provide a new team if traded -- not their likelihood of actually being dealt. That said, we did include our estimated percentage chances for each player to move, weaving in what we're hearing. Jeremy shared the latest buzz on each player, while Matt broke down what he sees on the tape. We even included some interesting team fits for each candidate. Some players have better odds of changing cities than others on the list, but all 25 are at the very least being discussed in trade conversations. Let's dive in. Jump to the top-ranked: QB | RB | WR | TE | OL Edge | DT | LB | CB | S 1. Jonathan Taylor , RB, Indianapolis Colts What Fowler is hearing: Teams I've talked to aren't totally sold that Indianapolis will trade Taylor despite heavy interest -- at least not yet. He is signed long term and would be a boon for next year's coaching staff, whether it's the current group or entirely new. But what Kenneth Walker III has done for Kansas City shows how a premier running back can put on new jersey colors and immediately reimagine a team's season. And the tenor of Indy's season is getting ugly, which affects all key players and could spark even more movement. Predicted chance of getting traded: 30% What Bowen sees on tape: Taylor is averaging 109.3 total yards per game this season, and he's tied for first in rushing TDs with eight. He's a volume runner with home run speed and pass-catching ability on screens and swings. His 17 rushes for 10 or more yards are tied for the fourth most in the league. Taylor would be an immediate upgrade for a team in need of a lead back who is decisive with the ball. Team fits: Seahawks, Commanders, Saints, Broncos, Vikings 2. Brian Thomas Jr ., WR, Jacksonville Jaguars What Fowler is hearing: League execs are sensing the end for BTJ in Jacksonville, as his targets and playing time have dipped. How Jacksonville has struggled to make this relationship work is still a mystery. Thomas is an elite mover with size who draws coverage deep, setting the stage for teammates Parker Washington and Jakobi Meyers to eat underneath. But that plan for Thomas hasn't materialized this season. And teams are circling with interest. Kansas City and Pittsburgh are among those exploring receiver help. Predicted chance of getting traded: 45% What Bowen sees on tape: Thomas' numbers have declined over the past two seasons, but he has the traits to still draw interest. At 6-foot-3 and 209 pounds, Thomas has the profile of an X receiver who can separate at multiple levels of the field. I see legit straight-line speed and ball-tracking ability. He had 87 receptions and 10 touchdowns as a rookie in 2024, but he has been limited to a 9-105-1 line so far this season. Team fits: Chiefs, Steelers, 49ers 3. Josh Sweat , Edge, Arizona Cardinals What Fowler is hearing: Rival teams could see him getting moved. "Sweat to Dallas makes a lot of sense to me," an NFC exec said. "That's a profile fit." Rumblings persist that Sweat would want a new contract -- he's in the second year of a four-year, $76 million deal -- and that could complicate things. But many teams are looking for an edge rusher. Predicted chance of getting traded: 40% What Bowen sees on tape: A long, angular mover who can win with speed-to-power, Sweat had 12 sacks and 37 pressures in Arizona last season. But his numbers haven't been as solid in 2026, with two sacks and 10 pressures. Still, Sweat's ability to threaten the edges of offensive tackles with his quickness off the ball fits pass-rush fronts across the league. Team fits: Cowboys, Bears, 49ers 4. Yaya Diaby , Edge, Tampa Bay Buccaneers What Fowler is hearing: Tampa Bay beat Carolina handedly in Week 7 , with Diaby exploding for three sacks. A loss would have put the Bucs at 1-6 and closer to dealing mode. Diaby, 27, is still on the radar, though, because Tampa is not poised to pay the 2027 free agent, and the emergence of second-year rusher David Walker (four sacks) gives the Bucs a natural replacement. Diaby needs a new contract, but an acquiring team could get a compensatory pick for him if he signs a substantial deal with another team in free agency. Predicted chance of getting traded: 35% What Bowen sees on tape: Diaby is a powerful and physical edge rusher with the temperament to set the edge against the run. He has three sacks and six tackles for loss in 2026, and he had 40 or more pressures in each of his past two seasons (with 11.5 total sacks over that time). He should be viewed as a quality starter. Team fits: Browns, Seahawks, Cowboys 5. Jerry Jeudy , WR, Cleveland Browns What Fowler is hearing: The Browns are not actively sending out feelers on Jeudy, but they would at least consider a substantial offer. Key word here is "substantial," though. I'm not sure, say, a fourth-round pick would move anyone in Cleveland, for example. Jeudy is part of the Browns' three-receiver sets and the veteran in that room for a good team in the playoff hunt. That dynamic diminishes his chances of being dealt. But as always, teams are looking for receiver help. Predicted chance of getting traded: 20% What Bowen sees on tape: Jeudy has the route traits and stop-start speed to separate as a multilevel route runner. He's sudden at the break point. However, the inconsistent hands have been an issue as a pro (33 career drops), and Jeudy lacks the frame and physicality to win on 50-50 throws. Jeudy had a career-best 1,229 receiving yards in 2024, yet he has just 16 receptions this season. Team fits: Chiefs, Raiders, Commanders 6. Daron Payne , DT, Washington Commanders What Fowler is hearing: Washington dealt key defensive pieces at the deadline three years ago and could be faced with a similar predicament this time with Payne, who's 29 and still has value. Payne is a 2027 free agent with a $16.4 million base this year. But the NFC East is also winnable, despite Washington's 1-4-1 record, so that could be a point in favor of the Commanders keeping him. Jacksonville is a potential fit, with some in the league noting the Jaguars could use a versatile interior player with pass-rush ability and have looked for that since the offseason. Predicted chance of getting traded: 25% What Bowen sees on tape: Payne can still provide an interior presence due to his foot quickness and strength in one-on-one matchups, plus he will impact the run game from multiple alignments. He had a career-best 11.5 sacks in 2022, but he has totaled only 12 over his past four seasons. Team fits: Jaguars, Giants, Buccaneers 7. Khalil Mack , Edge, Los Angeles Chargers What Fowler is hearing: Mack is productive and affordable. The Chargers gave him a $10 million signing bonus in March, so a new team would inherit the prorated version of his $8 million salary to close out his one-year deal. Returning to the Bears is a natural fit for the equivalent of a quality Day 3 pick. The Chargers have held off trading pieces such as Mack up to this point, though. Predicted chance of getting traded: 35% What Bowen sees on tape: Mack doesn't display the same level of explosive speed on tape, but he can still disrupt the pocket due to his play strength and advanced counter moves. Mack has 14.5 sacks and 83 pressures over his past three seasons, and he can play as both a pass-rushing linebacker or defensive end with third-down upside. Team fits: Bears, Browns, Bills, Cowboys 8. Riq Woolen , CB, Philadelphia Eagles What Fowler is hearing: When I talk to rival teams about which players Philly might move, Woolen's name comes up fairly often. He's a high-upside corner and 2027 free agent whose $1.26 million base salary could help facilitate a trade (much of his $12 million in guarantees came via signing or restructured bonuses). Predicted chance of getting traded: 35% What Bowen sees on tape: Woolen has the length and long speed at 6-foot-4 to help a defense majoring in man coverage and two-deep zone. The tackling and eye discipline could improve, but Woolen is a disruptor on the perimeter. In five pro seasons, he has 12 interceptions and 57 pass breakups. Team fits: Lions, Panthers, Steelers 9. Budda Baker , S, Arizona Cardinals What Fowler is hearing: A few wins won't camouflage Arizona's transitional state -- and it needs draft capital to finish the rebuild. Baker, who has seven consecutive Pro Bowls and has 3.5 sacks on the season, could help get the Cardinals some extra picks. Long a favorite in coaching circles, Baker would garner strong interest. He's owed $16.2 million this year and $17.8 million next year. People I've talked to believe the Cardinals should try to get something for Baker. Predicted chance of getting traded: 35% What Bowen sees on tape: With his downhill speed and urgency to the ball, Baker remains a disruptive safety who can play in split-field schemes or roam near the line of scrimmage. He isn't a high-level playmaker in coverage (nine career interceptions), but his ability to defend the run and blitz creates an impact in the game plan. Team fits: Bills, Jaguars 10. Patrick Queen , LB, Pittsburgh Steelers What Fowler is hearing: Rumors of a Queen trade persisted in the spring, with the Cowboys among teams that checked on his availability. He's also a 2027 free agent. But the Steelers' status as a 5-2 team likely keeps him in Pittsburgh. Predicted chance of getting traded: 20% What Bowen sees on tape: Queen is a run-and-hit defender with lateral pursuit speed. He can track the ball on the perimeter and close quickly on underneath throws as a zone defender. Queen struggles at times as a run defender in tight quarters, and his route identification can improve, but he has had at least 115 tackles in each of his four previous seasons. And he has 26 pass breakups over the past five years. Team fits: Cowboys, Bills 11. Jermaine Johnson II , Edge, Tennessee Titans What Fowler is hearing: Teams in the market for an edge rusher believe Johnson could be available at the right price. The Titans are reeling at 1-6 and are still in rebuilding mode, which necessitates adding more draft picks. Johnson is a Robert Saleh favorite from their Jets days together and just got to Tennessee via an offseason trade . But enough interest in the edge-rush market could make him a factor. Teams I talked to consider him a toss-up to be traded. Predicted chance of getting traded: 30% What Bowen sees on tape: I don't see elite traits with Johnson, but he has the play strength and length to dent the pocket, and he will pick up second-reaction hits on the quarterback due to his effort level. Plus, Johnson will hammer the ball back inside when setting edges as a run defender. Johnson has 16 career sacks over five pro seasons. Team fits: Browns, Bears 12. Landon Dickerson , G, Philadelphia Eagles What Fowler is hearing: Something feels off between the Eagles and Dickerson, one of the holdovers from the Jeff Stoutland offensive front. He recently took what appeared to be a passive-aggressive shot at the front office over his long-term outlook with the franchise. The Eagles are in a position to recoup draft capital for the future and are going younger on the offensive line. A mix of erratic play and injuries could affect his value, but he has Pro Bowl traits, his guarantees run dry next year, and he held up well in his return for "Monday Night Football" against the Cowboys . Predicted chance of getting traded: 25% What Bowen sees on tape: A Week 1 injury sent Dickerson to injured reserve, but he returned this past Monday. And when healthy, Dickerson can move defenders off the ball as a run blocker in both zone and gap schemes, and he can set an anchor in pass protection to handle power down his middle with his 6-6, 332-pound frame. In five seasons with the Eagles, Dickerson has a pass block win rate of 93.9%. Team fits: Chargers, Packers 13. Josh Downs , WR, Indianapolis Colts What Fowler is hearing: The Colts opened the floodgates with the Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner deals, and Downs -- the team's best receiver with Alec Pierce out -- has garnered interest from multiple teams. He's a 2027 free agent and would probably welcome the chance to play with someone like Patrick Mahomes if the Chiefs were to come calling, due to the Colts' sagging passing game. (Update: Downs requested a trade on Wednesday morning .) Predicted chance of getting traded: 45% What Bowen sees on tape: Downs has the sudden footwork and coverage recognition to uncover between the numbers. In four pro seasons with the Colts, he has 224 receptions and 11 touchdowns. He fits a team looking for a high-percentage target to win underneath and move the chains. Team fits: Chiefs, Steelers 14. Donte Jackson , CB, Los Angeles Chargers What Fowler is hearing: Corner is a position of need for several teams, and the Chargers likely could get a draft pick for Jackson. The 30-year-old has ball production and a reasonable contract -- a $6 million base salary. Plus, he is set to hit free agency in March. Predicted chance of getting traded: 25% What Bowen sees on tape: With his backfield vision and short-area closing speed, Jackson fits best as a zone corner. He's a top-down defender with route awareness who can create on-the-ball production. Jackson has 23 interceptions and 68 pass breakups over his career. Team fits: Panthers, Lions, Ravens 15. Shemar Stewart , Edge, Cincinnati Bengals What Fowler is hearing: While the Bengals typically don't trade away recently drafted players, Stewart is out of the defensive end rotation and would have value. He was inactive Sunday in Baltimore . He has high upside and turns 23 in November. The emergence of rookie Cashius Howell gives Cincinnati cover should it move on, too. Stewart is a name a few teams have had circled as a possibility for weeks, and teams predict a Day 3 pick would be the most likely value. Predicted chance of getting traded: 35% What Bowen sees on tape: Stewart has played just eight snaps this season, so teams would be betting on potential with the 2025 first-rounder. Stewart is an explosive mover with the physical profile to play on the edge, but he has yet to develop a refined pass-rush plan. He has two career sacks. Team fits: Eagles, Lions 16. Jauan Jennings , WR, Minnesota Vikings What Fowler is hearing: The Vikings' free agent addition is not a focal point of the offense and is considered a trade candidate leaguewide. But he did catch two passes for 34 yards Sunday against the Colts for a Minnesota passing game that's not exactly thriving right now. Jennings, who's on a one-year deal, could prove a low-cost option for teams looking to add to their receiver room. The 49ers are an obvious fit. Predicted chance of getting traded: 50% What Bowen sees on tape: Jennings has seen very limited opportunities in Minnesota this season, catching just four of eight targets. However, he has proved to be a reliable target in previous seasons. He's a consistent route runner who plays through contact and makes himself available to the quarterback on in-breaking targets. Team fits: Rams, Falcons, 49ers 17. Chris Godwin Jr ., WR, Tampa Bay Buccaneers What Fowler is hearing: Godwin is a legacy Buc through 10 seasons, but he hasn't been quite the same since his 2024 ankle injury . His veteran presence and savvy play could help another team. He's due $22 million in cash this year, which could be a deterrent to a deal, though. Predicted chance of getting traded: 15% What Bowen sees on tape: Godwin has yet to top 50 receiving yards in a game this season, and his play speed is declining. However, he still has value as a slot target with outside flex. He can use his coverage awareness to find open grass. And Godwin is willing to work the heavy traffic areas of the field on middle-of-the-field concepts. Team fits: Chiefs, Commanders 18. Rashod Bateman , WR, Baltimore Ravens What Fowler is hearing: This one is a bit of a wild card, as the Ravens aren't overly deep at receiver. But Bateman has long been a bit miscast in Baltimore. He's not a focal point of the offense -- he's more of a secondary option who can clear out to lift safeties -- but he would probably like to be featured more. Teams have had interest in the past, and rookie Ja'Kobi Lane is well-positioned for WR2 status in Baltimore. Predicted chance of getting traded: 15% What Bowen sees on tape: Bateman fits as a perimeter target with separation speed and ball-tracking ability to win on third-level throws and in-breakers. He can be re-routed, and he isn't a contested-catch specialist, but he fits as a No. 3 target with the ability to play Z or X. Bateman has 16 touchdown receptions in his career. Team fits: Commanders, Chiefs 19. Jackson Powers-Johnson , G, Las Vegas Raiders What Fowler is hearing: Johnson-Powers was benched in Week 6 and would probably welcome a change at this point. Several teams are combing the guard market, and Powers-Johnson wouldn't cost as much as the marquee names. A Day 3 pick swap might get something done, allowing the Raiders to improve positioning on the back of the draft order. Predicted chance of getting traded: 35% What Bowen sees on tape: Powers-Johnson has the traits to play both center and guard, and he had a 93.3% pass block win rate as a rookie in 2024. However, he was limited to eight games last season due to an ankle injury , and his 2026 tape shows a regression as a run blocker (career-low 62.7% run block win rate). Teams that had a high draft grade on Powers-Johnson could try to make a move here. Team fits: Jaguars, Chargers 20. Quentin Johnston , WR, Los Angeles Chargers What Fowler is hearing: Teams have considered Johnston a trade candidate dating back to March. The Chargers shut that down at the time and even exercised his fifth-year option. But the Chargers' 0-6 plight is resurfacing his name in league circles. Predicted chance of getting traded: 25% What Bowen sees on tape: With his physical tools at 6-3 and 208 pounds, plus the straight-line speed to create explosives, Johnston can help a team as a No. 3 receiver. The drops have been an issue in his four-year career (11 total), and he has been limited to only eight receptions this season. However, Johnston has 18 career touchdowns, and he produced 700 or more receiving yards in both 2024 and 2025. Team fits: 49ers, Raiders, Steelers 21. A'Shawn Robinson , DT, Tampa Bay Buccaneers What Fowler is hearing: Robinson is a name that a few teams floated to me because he's still a productive interior player and a veteran who could help a contending team. He also wouldn't cost much to acquire at this stage. He has played for four other teams -- the Lions, Rams, Panthers and Giants -- so he has coaching friends all over the league. Predicted chance of getting traded: 30% What Bowen sees on tape: At 6-3 and 320 pounds, Robinson is a powerful run defender who can play as a 1-technique nose or 3-technique defensive tackle. While Robinson doesn't provide pass-rushing upside (16 career sacks), he can push the interior of the pocket. He's an early-down defender who could help out a defensive line rotation. He even has two interceptions this season! Team fits: Rams, Ravens, Giants 22. Kirk Cousins , QB, Las Vegas Raiders What Fowler is hearing: Cousins played well enough through seven games that he has trade value. So does his contract, which after being reworked features a $1.3 million base salary. Aidan O'Connell , the Raiders' QB3, is a former starter who could slide into the primary backup role to Fernando Mendoza if Las Vegas is ready to start the rookie. There are no glaring needs at quarterback leaguewide, but injuries happen every week. The Raiders have not planned to be overly active at the deadline. Predicted chance of getting traded: 20% What Bowen sees on tape: What Bowen sees on tape: He's a pocket thrower who wins with timing and ball location. Cousins can read it out post-snap and play as a ball distributor. He lacks the mobility to make plays outside of structure at a consistent rate, but he can get to the edges on boot concepts, and he fits best in a system that incorporates play-action elements. Cousins has thrown 16 touchdown passes and five interceptions this season. Team fits: Panthers, Giants, Vikings 23. Cesar Ruiz , G, New Orleans Saints What Fowler is hearing: The Saints could explore trade options while sitting at 2-5, and several teams are looking for a quality guard. New Orleans has to win and already lost a starting offensive lineman in tackle Kelvin Banks Jr ., so this is hardly a slam dunk. But he's an intriguing name about whom teams could inquire. Predicted chance of getting traded: 25% What Bowen sees on tape: Ruiz is a capable player in pass protection, using his foot quickness and technique to slow interior rushers. He has posted a pass block win rate of 90% or better in five of seven pro seasons. However, Ruiz isn't a natural displacer at the point of attack in the run game, which impacts his ability to create consistent movement. His career run block win rate sits at 66.8%. Team fits: Lions, Commanders 24. Tony Pollard , RB, Tennessee Titans What Fowler is hearing: Several teams could use a running back, and Pollard is an attractive fallback plan if the Colts stand pat on Taylor. But as one AFC exec pointed out, "I don't think [the Titans] want to take weapons away from the quarterback right now." Indeed, Cam Ward needs his supporting cast in an important second season. His three-touchdown performance Sunday vs. Cleveland shows his value in Tennessee. Predicted chance of getting traded: 15% What Bowen sees on tape: Pollard is a slasher. With change-of-direction ability and vision to find daylight, he had his best day of the season in Week 7, producing 155 total yards against the Browns' defense. Pollard's receiving traits have been minimized in a struggling Titans offense this season, but he had 30 or more catches in each of his previous five seasons. He's a dual-threat back who could step into a lead role -- if the Titans decided to make a move. Team fits: Commanders, Vikings 25. Alontae Taylor , CB, Tennessee Titans What Fowler is hearing: Taylor is not an easy player to trade because of his contract, which guarantees his entire 2027 salary of $20.5 million. But as one NFC exec put it, Taylor was the best corner in free agency in March, and that type of player has value no matter what. Predicted chance of getting traded: 10% What Bowen sees on tape: Taylor has gotten off to a slow start with the Titans after signing in free agency. However, he plays a premium position, and he has the speed to cover receivers on the perimeter or play a disruptive role in the slot. In his four seasons with the Saints before joining Tennessee, Taylor had four interceptions, 40 pass breakups and seven sacks. Team fits: Bears, Steelers Honorable mentions Vita Vea , DT, Tampa Bay Buccaneers Tuli Tuipulotu , Edge, Los Angeles Chargers Kenny Gainwell , RB, Tampa Bay Buccaneers Jacoby Brissett , QB, Arizona Cardinals Grover Stewart , DT, Indianapolis Colts Kayvon Thibodeaux , Edge, New York Giants Dallas Goedert , TE, Philadelphia Eagles Alvin Kamara , RB, New Orleans Saints Andrew Wylie , G, Washington Commanders Josh Uche , Edge, Miami Dolphins Jessie Bates III , S, Atlanta Falcons Braden Smith , OT, Houston Texans Hollywood Brown , WR, Philadelphia Eagles Stefon Diggs , WR, Washington Commanders Cole Holcomb , LB, Pittsburgh Steelers Ja'Tavion Sanders , TE, Carolina Panthers

teamStories.detailText: (Photo by Ian Maule/Getty Images) | Getty Images Tuesday, the Las Vegas Raiders released third-year defensive tackle Jonah Laulu. After playing 67.9 percent of the defensive snaps last season, his play time dwindled to 32 percent and he was inactive twice. Let’s look at the position as the team moves on from Laulu: Tonka Hemingway: The 2025 fourth-round pick has been the Raiders’ leading snap getter at the position when healthy. In the first four weeks his snap percentage rate ranged from 52 to 73 percent. He was injured in Week 5 and missed Week 6. He was eased back into action, playing 29 percent of the snaps in Week 7. He has 15 tackles and one sack. Adam Butler: The veteran is averaging 51 percent snap play. He logged 70 percent of the snaps in Week 7, his most of the season. He is definitely a too-of-the-rotation defensive tackle. He has 18 tackles and a half of sack. Foley Fatukasi: Fatukasi, signed in training camp, has become a solid contributor. He’ playing 44 percent of the snaps. He has 12 tackles and a half a sack. Thomas Booker: He was a healthy scratch in Week 7 after he played in the first six games. His snap percentage rate ranged from 32 to 50 percent. It will be interesting to see if he remains inactive in the coming weeks. J.J. Pegues: The 2025 sixth-round draft pick has been active for three games, including the past two. He is averaging 13 percent of the snaps. He forced a fumble in Week 7. It wouldn’t be a surprise if he remains active on game days. Tim Keenan: The rookie — he was drafted in the seventh round by the Rams and signed to the Raiders’ practice squad in September after he was cut — is still on the practice squad.
